column15: Case overview: The case involves two criminal miscellaneous cases (Crl.M.C. Nos. 1279 and 1453 of 2016) filed by Mr. Sandeep P. Mehta and others against the State of Kerala, seeking to quash the proceedings in C.C. No. 2007/2015 pending before the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-I, Kozhikode. The complaint alleges violations of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act) concerning the sale of nicotine chewing gum. Key facts: 1. The complaint was filed by the Food Safety Officer under Section 42(5) of the FSS Act, alleging violations of Sections 3(i)(zz)(v), 26(1)(2)(i), and 59 of the FSS Act, along with Regulation 2.3.4 of the Food Safety Standards (Prohibition and Restriction of Sales) Regulation 2011. 2. An inspection on 02.04.2014 led to the purchase of nicotine chewing gum from M/s. Empee Credit Corporation, which was later tested and found to contain nicotine, deemed unsafe under the FSS Act. 3. The nicotine chewing gum was manufactured under a valid drug manufacturing license issued under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners argue that nicotine chewing gum is classified as a drug and not food, thus exempting it from prosecution under the FSS Act. 2. They contend that the product was manufactured and labeled in compliance with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, including necessary warnings and declarations. 3. The Public Prosecutor argued that the petitioners lacked authorization to sell the product and that the nicotine content constituted a violation of the FSS Act. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the definition of 'food' under the FSS Act explicitly excludes drugs and medicinal products. 2. The court found that the nicotine chewing gum was manufactured and distributed as a drug, supported by the presence of a valid license and appropriate labeling. 3. The court concluded that the allegations did not establish that the product was offered for sale as food, thus the FSS Act was not applicable. 4. The court also stated that any violation related to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act would require prosecution by specified officers, which did not include the Food Safety Officer. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the Crl.M.C.s, quashing the complaint and all further proceedings in C.C. No. 2007/2015, determining that the prosecution was not legally sustainable under the FSS Act.

- The petitioner, A.G.Rajendran, is the accused No.1 in S.T.C.No.204 of 2022, seeking to quash the proceedings against him.

- On 25 August 2020, Food Safety Officers took samples of "Winner Refined Palmolein Oil" from the petitioner‚Äôs shop.

- The petitioner argued that the Designated Officer failed to dispose of the appeal and did not forward the sample to a referral laboratory, violating the Food Safety and Standards Act.

Sathish and Shiva Kumar, who worked as Food Safety Officers and designated officers, respectively, in Karnataka's Food Safety and Standards Department. Both petitioners initially joined as Food Inspectors through direct recruitment in 2003 and were later appointed as Food Safety Officers by the government. Shiva Kumar was also appointed as a designated officer, with the government issuing notifications for such appointments, including a notification dated 24.01.2017 appointing Medical Officers as designated officers. The petitioners challenged these appointments, arguing that they were contrary to rules that specified a 50% direct recruitment and 50% promotion method for filling designated officer posts, and that the appointment of Medical Officers violated these rules. They also contended that the appointments conflicted with earlier orders and the judgment passed in previous writ petitions. The respondents defended the appointments, stating they were made on an ad hoc basis in public interest due to a lack of staff, pending the framing and implementation of proper recruitment rules. The tribunal dismissed the petitions, ruling that the appointments were temporary and in public interest, and that the petitioners' existing roles and salaries were unaffected. The petitioners argued that the appointments were improper and against rules and prior orders, while the respondents maintained they were necessary interim measures.

column15: Case overview: The case involves two writ petitions filed by H.N. Sathish and Shiva Kumar against the State of Karnataka and others, challenging a common order dated November 2, 2020, from the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal. The Tribunal dismissed their applications contesting a notification from January 24, 2017, which appointed 36 district level officers as designated officers under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The petitioners argue that the appointment was contrary to established recruitment rules. Key facts: 1. The petitioners were initially appointed as Food Inspectors in 2003 and later as Food Safety Officers in 2011. 2. The Karnataka government issued notifications in 2014 and 2015 appointing the petitioners as Designated Officers on an additional charge basis. 3. The Health and Family Welfare Service (Food Safety and Standard Department) (Recruitment) Rules, 2015, stipulate that 50% of designated officer posts should be filled by direct recruitment and 50% by promotion. 4. The January 24, 2017 notification appointed Medical Officers as Designated Officers, which the petitioners contested. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners argue that the notification is against the recruitment rules and previous court orders. 2. They claim the appointment of Medical Officers as Designated Officers is not permissible under the rules. 3. The respondents contend that the notification was issued in public interest due to a shortage of enforcement authorities and was an adhoc arrangement until the rules could be fully implemented. column3: The petitioner, Arvind Kumar, is challenging a criminal proceeding initiated against him under section 27(b) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act related to a case involving the sale of a supplement product called Instasam 200 tablets by INTAS Pharmaceuticals Private Limited, Ranchi. The complaint was filed after inspection revealed that the product's label did not mention the drug manufacturing license number and instead labeled it as a dietary supplement. The government analyst's report indicated that the product appeared to be a drug, which was under dispute as the petitioner claimed that the product was a food item authorized under a license under the Food Safety and Standards Act. The respondent, The State of Jharkhand, supported the proceeding, arguing that the product was a drug and the order of cognizance was proper. The petitioners argued that the proceedings should be quashed due to violations of legal procedures, lack of specific responsible persons, and the fact that the petitioner and managing director did not look into the daily affairs of the company, thus not liable. They also claimed that they held a valid license under the Food Safety and Standards Act for the supplement. The court ultimately found that the proceedings were an abuse of process and quashed the case.

column15: Case overview: The case involves two criminal miscellaneous petitions (Cr.M.P. No. 266 of 2014 and Cr.M.P. No. 486 of 2014) filed by Arvind Kumar and Kiran Mazumdar Shaw, respectively, against the State of Jharkhand. The petitions seek to quash the entire criminal proceedings, including an order dated September 16, 2013, taking cognizance under Section 27(b) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, in connection with C-III Case No. 271/2013. The complaints allege violations related to the labeling and classification of a product, Instasam 200 tablets, as a drug without proper licensing. Key facts: 1. A complaint was filed by the State after an inspection of INTAS Pharmaceuticals, which revealed that the product's labeling did not include the required Drug Manufacturing License number. 2. The product was claimed to treat various medical conditions, leading to the conclusion by the Government Analyst that it qualifies as a drug under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. 3. The petitioners argue that the Managing Director cannot be held vicariously liable without specific allegations of involvement in the company's day-to-day operations. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners contend that the complaint lacks necessary averments to establish vicarious liability under Section 34 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. 2. They argue that the product should be classified as a dietary supplement, which is excluded from the definition of drugs under the Food Safety and Standards Act. 3. The petitioners assert that their right to have the sample analyzed in a Central Laboratory was violated, as required by Section 23(4)(iii) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. 4. The State's counsel argues that the analyst's conclusion was justified and that the cognizance taken by the court was appropriate. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the complaint did not provide sufficient details to establish the Managing Director's responsibility for the alleged offense. 2. It emphasized that the product's classification as a drug was based solely on the insert provided, without independent analysis. 3. The court highlighted the importance of adhering to statutory provisions, particularly Section 23(4)(iii), which was not followed in this case. 4. The court found that allowing the proceedings to continue would constitute an abuse of process of law. Decision or judgment: The court quashed the entire criminal proceeding, including the cognizance order dated September 16, 2013, under Section 27(b) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, in connection with C-III Case No. 271/2013, and vacated any interim orders.

column3: The petitioners were convicted of offenses related to food safety laws in a case arising from the testing of milk samples. The samples were sent to both the State Laboratory and the Central Laboratory for analysis; the State Laboratory reported the milk as substandard, while the Central Laboratory reported it as substandard and un-safe. The petitioner's representative claimed that formalin had been added to the milk sample to preserve it, but this fact was only communicated to the State Laboratory and not to the Central Laboratory. During cross-examination, it was revealed that the sample's formalin content was not disclosed to the Central Laboratory, which affected the test results. The petitioners sought permission to summon an expert to explain the consequences of this nondisclosure, but their application was dismissed by the appellate court, which considered that the issue could have been raised earlier and that the petitioners did not specify the facts in their initial petition. The petitioners argued that examining an expert was necessary and should be permitted, as it would not delay the proceedings, but the court found no grounds to interfere with the appellate court's decision.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a criminal petition filed by Nandi Kondala Rao and others against the State of Andhra Pradesh concerning their conviction under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The petitioners were convicted in C.C.No.185 of 2014 by the Judicial Civil Judge-cum-Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Vinukonda, for various offenses related to food safety. They subsequently appealed the conviction in Crl.Appeal.No.64 of 2019 before the Principal District & Session Judge, Guntur. During the appeal, the petitioners sought to summon an expert witness, which was denied by the Appellate Court, prompting this petition. Key facts: 1. The petitioners were convicted for offenses under Sections 3(1)(zz)(iii)(xi), 26(2)(i), 27(1), and 59(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. 2. The milk sample in question was analyzed by both the State Laboratory and the Central Laboratory, with differing results regarding its safety. 3. The petitioners argued that the Central Laboratory was not informed that formalin had been mixed in the milk sample, which affected the test results. 4. The Appellate Court dismissed the petitioners' application to summon an expert witness, stating that the issues could have been raised during the trial. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners contended that the Appellate Court's rejection of their application to summon an expert was unjust, as it was crucial for explaining the discrepancies in the test results. 2. They argued that a liberal interpretation of Section 391 of the Cr.P.C. should allow for the examination of the expert witness without causing significant delay in the appeal process. 3. The Public Prosecutor countered that the petition did not raise the issue of formalin not being disclosed to the Central Laboratory and that the application was filed too late. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the Appellate Court had dismissed the application based on the lack of relevant facts in the petition and that the issues raised in the current petition were not previously considered. 2. The court found no reason to interfere with the Appellate Court's order, as the petitioners failed to provide sufficient grounds for summoning the expert witness. 3. The court emphasized that the petitioners had ample opportunity to present their case during the trial and appeal stages. Decision or judgment: The court dismissed the criminal petition, upholding the Appellate Court's decision to reject the application to summon an expert witness. There was no order as to costs, and any pending miscellaneous petitions were closed.

column3: The case involves two petitioners, S. Bagyalakshmi and S. Balamurugan, who are accused of selling unsafe food. The prosecution's case is that during a routine inspection on April 4, 2014, the Food Safety Officer seized a food sample and sent it for analysis, which confirmed the food was unsafe. The Food Safety Officer requested and received sanction from the Commissioner to prosecute the petitioners on September 26, 2014. The complaint was filed on August 24, 2016, more than two years after the sample analysis and after the sanction was granted. The petitioners argued that the complaint was filed outside the statutory time limit of one year, with no extension granted, and that the delay was due to confusion over jurisdiction. The court found that the complaint was filed beyond the allowed time and that no extension was obtained from the Commissioner, leading to the quashing of the case.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a Criminal Original Petition filed by S. Bagyalakshmi and S. Balamurugan against the State of Tamil Nadu, represented by the Food Safety Officer, seeking to quash the proceedings in C.C.No.3505 of 2016 before the XVII Metropolitan Magistrate, Saidapet, Chennai. The petitioners were accused of selling unsafe food. Key facts: 1. A routine inspection was conducted on 04.04.2014, during which unsafe food was identified, and a sample was seized for analysis. 2. The analysis report confirming the food was unsafe was received on 16.04.2014. 3. The Food Safety Officer requested the Commissioner for sanction to prosecute on 22.05.2014, which was granted on 26.09.2014. 4. The complaint was filed on 24.08.2016, over two years after the sanction. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners argued that the complaint was filed beyond the one-year limitation period stipulated in Section 77 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which requires prosecution to be initiated within one year from the date of the offence. 2. They contended that no extension for filing the complaint was granted by the Commissioner, making the prosecution legally unsustainable. 3. The prosecution argued that delays were due to confusion regarding jurisdiction under the new law. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the complaint was filed well beyond the one-year limit, which should have been by 03.04.2015. 2. It emphasized that the Commissioner could approve an extension of up to three years, but no such approval was sought or granted. 3. The court found no merit in the prosecution's reasoning for the delay, stating that the prosecution could have sought clarification or extension from the Commissioner. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the Criminal Original Petition and quashed the proceedings in C.C.No.3505 of 2016, concluding that the complaint was filed beyond the statutory limitation period.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a complaint filed by Khem Singh, Food Safety Officer (FSO) of Northern Railway, against Pankaj Gupta and Shamshad Begum for violations under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act). The complaint was based on the sale of unsafe and sub-standard tomato sauce at a tea stall on November 26, 2016. The court delivered its judgment on December 20, 2022, convicting both accused. Key facts: 1. The FSO purchased a sample of tomato sauce from the tea stall operated by Pankaj Gupta. 2. The sample was analyzed and found to contain unpermitted coloring agents and was sub-standard in terms of total soluble solids and acidity. 3. The accused were given an opportunity to appeal the food analyst's report, which confirmed the findings. 4. The complaint was filed after obtaining necessary consent under Section 42 of the FSS Act. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed that the sauce was not sold directly but used with other food items. 2. The defense argued that Shamshad Begum, as a licensee, was not present during the sampling and should not be held liable. 3. The defense also contended that the sample collection process was flawed and that the food article was not for sale. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that both accused were responsible for the food safety violations as per the FSS Act. 2. The court ruled that the presence of synthetic coloring agents and the sub-standard nature of the sauce constituted violations of the Act. 3. The court dismissed the defense arguments regarding the absence of public witnesses and the cleanliness of the sample bottles, stating that the testimony of the FSO was credible. 4. The court emphasized that the licensee is responsible for the food safety of the products sold under their license. Decision or judgment: The court convicted both Pankaj Gupta and Shamshad Begum for violations under Sections 51 and 59 of the FSS Act. The case was set for a separate hearing on the point of sentence.

The petitioners contend that the Commissioner failed to provide written reasons for the delay in granting sanction. 3. The court emphasized that the Commissioner must provide written reasons for any delay in sanctioning prosecution, which was not done in this case. 3. The court found that the lack of justifiable reasons for the delay contravened the provisions of Section 77. Decision or judgment: The court quashed the proceedings in C.C. No. 12 of 2019 and C.C. column15: Case overview: The case involves Criminal Original Petitions filed by P.Panneer Selvam and V.Anbazhagan against Thiru.P.Jaganathan, a Food Safety Officer, seeking to quash criminal prosecutions in STC No.249 of 2016 and STC No.146 of 2016 for alleged violations of the Food Safety Standards Act, 2006. The petitions argue that the petitioners, as wholesalers and retailers, should not be held liable for the alleged offenses. Key facts: 1. The petitioners are associated with SVS Classic Foods, which is a wholesaler, stockist, and retailer of sago products. 2. On 10.10.2013, the respondent inspected the premises and took samples of sago powder for analysis. 3. Reports indicated violations of the Food Safety Standards, leading to private complaints filed on 25.01.2016 and 16.03.2016. 4. The petitioners argue that the prosecution was initiated beyond the statutory time limits set by the Food Safety and Standards Act. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners contend that they are not manufacturers and thus not liable for the alleged offenses. 2. They argue that the request for sanctioning prosecution was made beyond the mandatory period of fourteen days after receiving the food analysis report. 3. The complaints were filed beyond the one-year limit for prosecution as per Section 77 of the Act. 4. The petitioners assert that two separate complaints for the same contravention are not maintainable. 5. The respondent claims that the delay in prosecution was due to administrative reasons and that the two complaints are valid as they stem from separate samples. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the respondent failed to comply with the mandatory provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act regarding the timing of the prosecution. 2. The court noted that the request for sanctioning prosecution was made well beyond the fourteen-day limit after the analysis report was received. 3. The court highlighted that the complaints were filed beyond the one-year limit for prosecution, and the reasons provided for condoning the delay were insufficient. 4. The court concluded that two separate prosecutions for the same contravention were not permissible. Decision or judgment: The court allowed both original petitions and quashed the criminal prosecutions in STC No.249 of 2016 and STC No.146 of 2016, citing failure to follow mandatory requirements.

column3: The case involves a complaint filed by a Food Safety Officer against Tulsi Ram Aggarwal, who is the owner of M/s Aggarwal Sweets & Restaurants in Delhi Cantonment. On March 15, 2019, the Food Safety Officer purchased a 2 kg sample of "Laddu" from an open tray in the accused‚Äôs shop, which had no label declaration. The sample was collected using clean techniques, divided into four parts, and preserved with formalin, then sent to a food analyst and later to a referral laboratory for testing. The analysis revealed that the "Laddu" contained artificial colors exceeding the permitted limits, with a total dye content of 334.36 ppm, which is higher than the maximum of 100 ppm, making it unsafe for human consumption. The accused pleaded not guilty, and the court found that the sample was properly collected and analyzed, and that the food contained unsafe levels of artificial coloring. The issue of sample representativeness was addressed by the court, confirming the evidence was valid. The prosecutor argued that the results of the referral laboratory report replaced the initial analysis, and the court ultimately convicted the accused of selling unsafe food in violation of applicable provisions.

column3: The applicant, Beerbal Dhakad, is accused of being involved in offenses related to selling Paneer that was found to be unsafe for human consumption during an inspection by a Food Inspector. A complaint and an FIR were filed against him alleging offenses under Sections 420, 272, and 273 of the Indian Penal Code. The applicant disputes the charges, claiming the FIR is malicious and that his act falls under a specific law which limits his liability, particularly under the Food Safety and Standards Act. The applicant's shop was inspected by a Food Inspector, who seized Paneer deemed unsafe for human consumption under Section 3 (1) (zz) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA). 2. column15: Case overview: The case involves an appeal by Rajesh Subramaniam and Vijay Kumar against the Food Safety Officer and others regarding a penalty imposed for violations under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act). The appellants challenge an order dated November 18, 2021, which imposed a penalty of Rs. One Lakh for violations related to the presence of extraneous matter in food. The judgment was delivered on September 27, 2022, by Principal District & Sessions Judge Dharmesh Sharma. Key facts: 1. The appellants are directors of M/s. J.V. Restaurant Private Limited, operating 'The Town House Cafe'. 2. On March 9, 2018, a Food Safety Officer inspected the cafe and collected samples of 'Prepared Dal Tadka' for analysis. 3. A complaint was filed on October 1, 2018, alleging that the samples contained extraneous matter (vegetable oil), leading to the penalty. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The appellants argue that vegetable oil does not qualify as extraneous matter under Section 3 (1) (i) of the FSS Act. 2. They contend that the Food Safety Officer did not follow proper sampling guidelines and that the order was issued without summoning the chef. 3. The appellants assert that the use of vegetable oil is standard in cooking and does not constitute cheating or misbranding. 4. The respondents opposed the appeal but did not file a formal reply. Court's reasoning: 1. The court reviewed the definitions and provisions of the FSS Act, particularly regarding extraneous matter and the responsibilities of food business operators. 2. It noted that the Adjudicating Officer found no basis for classifying vegetable oil as extraneous matter and acknowledged that the food was not unsafe for consumption. 3. The court emphasized that the use of vegetable oil is common in cooking 'Dal Tadka' and cannot be deemed an extraneous matter. 4. The court concluded that the appellants had no reason to suspect that failing to disclose vegetable oil usage constituted an offense. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the appeal, quashing the penalty imposed by the Adjudicating Officer. The record was ordered to be sent back, and the appeal file was to be consigned to the Record Room.

Ltd., against an order dated 25.02.2022 from the Ld. Adjudicating Officer imposing penalties for violations of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act). The appellants challenge the penalties imposed for manufacturing misbranded food products. Key facts: 1. The Food Safety Officer collected samples of 'Mixed Fruit Jam' from M/s. The Leela Palace on 29.05.2017, which were found to be misbranded due to the failure to declare the percentage of ingredients on the label. 2. The Ld. ADM initially imposed a penalty of Rs. 60,000 on the appellants and Rs. 1,00,000 on the company for violations of the FSS Act and related regulations. 3. The case was previously remanded for a fresh hearing due to errors in the initial order regarding the penalties and violations cited. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The appellants argue that the penalties imposed on the company were unlawful as the company had previously been acquitted without penalty. 2. They contend that the samples were not analyzed by an accredited laboratory, rendering the analytical report invalid. 3. The appellants also claim that the Ld. ADM failed to compel the Food Analyst for cross-examination and misinterpreted the FSSAI's advisory on minor label offenses. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found no illegality in the Ld. ADM's approach and confirmed that the labeling violations were adequately established. 2. The court noted that the requirement to disclose ingredient percentages is mandatory for products like mixed fruit jam, especially when ingredients are emphasized on the label. 3. The court distinguished the current case from previous rulings cited by the appellants, affirming that the remand was appropriate for reassessing the company's liability. Decision or judgment: The appeal was dismissed, and the appellants were directed to comply with the penalties imposed by the Ld. ADM within 30 days. The interim stay on the order was vacated, and the record was to be returned to the Ld. ADM.

Case overview: The case involves a Criminal Original Petition filed by M/s Blue Planets Foods Pvt. Ltd. and its directors against the State, seeking to quash a complaint filed by the Food Safety Officer under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The complaint alleges that the restaurant served unsafe food containing prohibited color additives. The petitioners argue that the complaint is barred by limitation and that the directors are not liable as they were not involved in day-to-day management. The petition was heard by Dr. Justice G. Jayachandran in the High Court of Judicature at Madras. 

Key facts: 1. The Food Safety Officer inspected the restaurant on January 31, 2019, and drew samples of food for analysis. 2. The analysis report dated November 23, 2019, indicated that the food was unsafe due to the presence of prohibited color additives. 3. The petitioners were informed of the report and given the opportunity to appeal within 30 days, which they did not utilize. 4. The complaint was filed in court on December 31, 2020, after the Commissioner of Food Safety sanctioned prosecution on June 16, 2020. 

Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners argue that the complaint is barred by limitation as it was filed more than one year after the alleged offence. 2. They contend that the delay in the analysis report deprived them of the opportunity to seek a second opinion from a referral lab. 3. The petitioners claim that directors 2 to 6 were not involved in the management of the company and should not be held liable. 4. The respondent argues that the delay was justified and that the complaint was filed within the extended limitation period allowed by the Commissioner. 

Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the Food Analyst's inability to complete the analysis within the prescribed time was communicated and justified due to administrative reasons. 2. The court held that the time taken for analysis and the subsequent sanction for prosecution were within the limits set by the Food Safety and Standards Act. 3. The court emphasized that the directors are deemed guilty under Section 66 of the Act unless they can prove their lack of involvement or diligence in preventing the offence. 4. The court found that the petitioners did not provide sufficient evidence to support their claims of non-involvement in the management of the company. 

Decision or judgment: The court dismissed the Criminal Original Petition, ruling that the complaint was not barred by limitation and that the directors could be held liable under the Food Safety and Standards Act. The court upheld the validity of the prosecution against the petitioners.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a complaint filed by Ranjeet Singh, Food Safety Officer, against Sh. Chandra Bhushan Jha, Sh. D. S. Rana, M/s Himalya Hospitality Pvt. Ltd., and Sh. Ravijot Singh for violations under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA). The complaint was based on an incident that occurred on September 3, 2014, where food samples were taken from M/s Himalya Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. and found to be unsafe for human consumption. The judgment was delivered on June 25, 2022, by Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Ms. Nabeela Wali. Key facts: 1. The complainant visited the premises of M/s Himalya Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. on September 3, 2014, and found food articles stored for sale without proper labeling. 2. A sample of Kaju pieces was taken for analysis, which was later found to be fungus contaminated and sub-standard. 3. The sample was sent to a food analyst and subsequently to a Referral Food Laboratory, which confirmed the presence of live insects and rancidity. 4. The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The prosecution argued that the sample was unsafe due to contamination and that the accused failed to rebut the findings of the food analyst. 2. The defense contended that the sample proceedings were improperly conducted, and there were contradictions in witness testimonies. 3. The defense also argued that the sample was not representative and that the presence of insects could have occurred after the sample was taken. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the prosecution must establish that the food sample was unsafe for human consumption. 2. The court found that while the sample was sub-standard due to discolored units, there was insufficient evidence to prove it was unsafe at the time of sampling. 3. The court acknowledged the defense's arguments regarding the handling of the sample and the lack of preservatives. The court reduced the penalty from Rs.1,00,000 to Rs.50,000 per appellant.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a criminal appeal filed by M/S Himalayan Ales Private Limited and its Deputy Manager, Manish Saxena, against the State of Madhya Pradesh regarding a penalty imposed under the Food Safety and Standard Act, 2006. The appeal challenges the order dated 15/02/2021 from the District Judge and Appellate Tribunal, which confirmed the adjudicating authority's decision. Key facts: 1. The Food Safety Officer inspected the appellant's industrial unit on 20/09/2018 and found packets of rolled wheat used for beer production that lacked vegetarian or non-vegetarian labeling. 2. A sample was sent for analysis, which confirmed the product's quality but identified it as misbranded due to the absence of the required labeling. 3. A show cause notice was issued, and the appellants argued that they were the end users of the product and had not violated any provisions. 4. The Adjudicating Officer penalized the appellants under Section 52 of the Act, leading to the appeal. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The appellants contended that the penalties were illegal and that they could not be penalized for misbranding as they were not the manufacturers. 2. They argued that the penalty was imposed twice for a single act and that the sanction for prosecution was granted without proper consideration. 3. The State argued that the orders were lawful and justified. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the product was indeed misbranded as it lacked the necessary labeling, which is a violation of the Food Safety and Standard Act. 2. The court ruled that as a Food Business Operator, the appellant was responsible for ensuring compliance with the Act, regardless of being the end user. 3. The court confirmed that the sanction for prosecution was valid and that the penalties imposed were in accordance with the law. Decision or judgment: The court upheld the penalty for breach of Section 26(2)(ii) of the Food Safety and Standard Act but reduced the penalty from Rs.1,00,000 to Rs.50,000 for each appellant, totaling Rs.1,00,000. The appeal was partly allowed and disposed of.

Case overview: The case involves a Criminal Original Petition filed by Rajkumar against the Food Safety Officer, seeking to quash the proceedings in S.T.C. No. 7624 of 2021 pending before the Judicial Magistrate No.VI, Madurai. The petitioner contends that the prosecution is unsustainable as it pertains to lighting oil, which he argues does not fall under the definition of food as per the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The petition was heard on 29 August 2022 by Justice V. Sivagnanam. 

Key facts: 1. On 07.07.2022, the Food Safety Officer seized 370 Kilo Litres of Amudham Brand Lighting Oil and 110 Kilo Litres of Amudham Oil from the petitioner's shop. 2. The seized samples were sent to a Food Analyst, who reported on 10.09.2020 that the samples were misleading, misbranded, substandard, unsafe, and prohibited for sale. 3. The complaint against the petitioner was filed after obtaining sanction from the Commissioner of Food Safety. 4. The petitioner argues that lighting oil does not qualify as food under Section 3(J) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. 

Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner claims that the prosecution is barred as the product was seized after its expiry and that lighting oil is not intended for human consumption. 2. The respondent's counsel confirmed that the seized product is lighting oil, not edible oil. 3. The petitioner cites a circular from the Commissioner of Food Safety stating that lighting oil is not for edible use and thus not covered under the Act. 

Court's reasoning: 1. The court reviewed the definition of food under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which excludes non-edible items. 2. The court noted that the seized oil was confirmed to be lighting oil, which is not intended for human consumption. 3. The court found that the prosecution against the petitioner was unsustainable as the product does not fall under the definition of food. 

Decision or judgment: The court quashed the proceedings in S.T.C. No. 7624 of 2021 against the petitioner, allowing the Criminal Original Petition. The connected miscellaneous petitions were also closed.

column3: The petitioner, Sai Surya Enterprises, is a business that deals in cashew husk and cashew peel, which are used for purposes such as pigmentation, tanning, and pan masala. On December 20, 2021, respondents 3 and 4 seized 60 tonnes or 1600 bags of cashew husk powder from the petitioner's godown located in Duppalapudi Village, Anaparthy Mandal. The seizure occurred at around 2 p.m. when officials visited the premises and took a sample of 4 kg from one of the bags. The petitioner contends that the seized items are not food, not meant for human consumption, and are not adulterants, thus their seizure was illegal and arbitrary. The petitioner argued that the seized product is not a food item under the relevant law and is a general industrial product, not an adulterant used for preparing food for human consumption. The petitioner also mentioned that the seizure was based on suspicion and confessional statements but that there was no evidence that the seized cashew husk was used for adulterating any food. Respondent authorities claimed that the seizure was based on suspicion that the cashew husk powder was being used to manufacture spurious tea powder, and that it was seized as part of an investigation into offences under various sections of the law. The petitioner challenged the seizure, asserting it was illegal since the product is not a food item or adulterant and was being kept for sale for industrial purposes.

column15: Case overview: The writ petition was filed by Sai Surya Enterprises against the State of Andhra Pradesh, challenging the seizure of 60 tonnes (1600 bags) of cashew husk from their godown on December 20, 2021, as illegal and arbitrary. The petitioner sought a Writ of Mandamus to declare the actions of the respondents unlawful. Key facts: 1. The seizure occurred during an inspection by the Additional District Food Safety Officer and others, who took samples and locked the godown. 2. The petitioner was implicated in a separate case involving the seizure of adulterated tea powder, leading to their addition as an accused in Crime No. 277 of 2021. 3. The petitioner argued that cashew husk is not a food item as defined under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and is used for various industrial purposes. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner contended that the seized cashew husk is not an adulterant or food item under the Act and that its seizure violated their right to free trade under Article 19 of the Constitution of India. 2. The Government Pleader argued that the seizure was justified based on confessions linking the petitioner to the supply of cashew husk for making spurious tea powder. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the seized cashew husk is not a food item or adulterant as defined by the Act and is used for non-food purposes. 2. The court noted that the mere association of the petitioner with the adulteration case does not justify the seizure of the cashew husk. 3. The court referenced previous case law indicating that products available in the market cannot be seized solely based on their potential use for adulteration. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the writ petition, declaring the seizure of the cashew husk illegal and arbitrary, and directed the authorities to release the seized stock to the petitioner immediately. No costs were awarded.

column3: The petitioner, Atul Saraf, is the owner of Pukhraj Enterprises, a firm involved in preparing and selling mava. The authorities inspected his premises on 9 November 2020 and found that he was producing and selling adulterated or impure mava for human consumption, instead of pure milk-based mava. Multiple previous cases had been registered against him for similar violations, and he was considered a habitual offender. A food safety officer lodged a complaint on 6 December 2020, leading to the registration of an FIR against him for offenses punishable under Sections 272 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code. The petitioner argued that there was no evidence to establish that he deceived or cheated anyone or that he intentionally misled consumers into purchasing adulterated mava, and contended that the matter should be governed by food safety laws rather than the IPC. The respondents maintained that there was sufficient material to proceed against him under the specified sections. The court ultimately found that no offense under Sections 272 and 420 was made out against the petitioner, as there was no evidence of deception, fraud, or inducement to part with property. The court also noted that provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, would apply, and the FIR was quashed.

Case overview
- The case is titled Atul Saraf vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh, heard in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh on May 21, 2024. 
- The petitioner, Atul Saraf, sought to quash an FIR registered against him for offences under Sections 272 and 420 of the IPC.

Key facts
- The FIR (Crime No. 459/2020) was based on an inspection conducted on November 9, 2020, at Pukhraj Enterprises, owned by the petitioner, where it was found that he was preparing and selling adulterated mava for human consumption.
- The Food Safety Officer lodged a complaint on December 6, 2020, leading to the FIR. The petitioner was described as a habitual offender with similar cases registered against him previously.

Legal issues and arguments
- The petitioner argued that no offence under Section 420 IPC was made out as there was no evidence of deception or cheating involved in the sale of adulterated mava. He contended that the matter should be governed by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which has precedence over IPC provisions regarding food safety.
- The respondent's counsel maintained that there was sufficient material to proceed with the case under both Sections 272 and 420 IPC, asserting that the FIR should not be quashed at this stage.

Court's reasoning
- The court examined the requirements for establishing an offence under Section 420 IPC, noting that there must be evidence of someone being deceived into delivering property or valuable security. The court found no such evidence in this case.
- The court referenced previous judgments, including Dinesh Sahu v. State of Madhya Pradesh and Ram Nath v. State of Uttar Pradesh, emphasizing that the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, provides comprehensive provisions for food safety offences and has an overriding effect over IPC provisions.
- The court concluded that the allegations against the petitioner, if taken at face value, did not constitute an offence under Section 420 IPC. Furthermore, the provisions of Section 272 IPC could not be invoked as the matter fell under the Food Safety and Standards Act.

Decision or judgment
- The court allowed the petition, quashing the FIR No. 459/2020 registered at Police Station Unhel for offences under Sections 272 and 420 IPC against the petitioner. 
- The respondents were granted the liberty to initiate appropriate proceedings under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, specifically for offences punishable under Section 59 of the Act.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a criminal petition filed by Mr. P V G Srinivasa Rao against the State of Telangana to quash C.C.No.996 of 2015, which was initiated for alleged violations of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The petition was filed under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The charges stemmed from a complaint by the Food Safety Officer regarding the sale of unsafe food products. Key facts: 1. On August 2, 2013, the Food Safety Officer purchased 2 kilograms of vegetable biryani from M/s. Reliance Super Market, which was later found to contain synthetic color, making it unsafe for consumption. 2. The officer followed proper procedures for sampling and analysis, with the report indicating the presence of unsafe additives received on August 14, 2013. 3. The complaint was filed on October 19, 2015, after obtaining sanction for prosecution. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argued that the complaint was filed beyond the one-year limitation period prescribed by Section 77 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, as the complaint was filed more than a year after the offense was committed. 2. The petitioner contended that the company (Reliance Super Market) was not made an accused, which is necessary for vicarious liability. 3. The petitioner claimed that there were no prescribed standards for vegetable biryani, making the complaint unwarranted. 4. The petitioner also argued that the sanction for prosecution was obtained after the stipulated four-month period. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the complaint was indeed filed beyond the one-year limitation period, as the offense was committed on August 2, 2013, and the complaint was filed on October 19, 2015. 2. The court emphasized that the limitation period should be calculated from the date of the analyst's report, which indicated the offense. 3. The court agreed with the petitioner that the company should have been made an accused for the prosecution to be valid. 4. The court referenced previous rulings that support the necessity of having the company as a party in cases involving corporate liability. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the criminal petition and quashed the proceedings in C.C.No.996 of 2015 against the petitioner-accused, stating that the complaint was filed beyond the limitation period and that the company was not included as an accused party. Consequently, any pending miscellaneous petitions were also closed.

column3: The petitioners, Goldripe International Pvt. Ltd., conducted business involving the use of Ethephon sachets for ripening fruits. The respondents, the State of Andhra Pradesh through respondent Nos. 1 and 2, issued a memo discouraging or interfering with the use of Ethephon (Ethylene ripener sachets), despite it being approved by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and not being banned. The petitioners argued that the use of Ethephon is safe, approved, and similar to previous ripening methods such as calcium carbide, which was banned in the 1970s. The petitioners also claimed that respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were encouraging the use of their product, En-ripe, or interfering with their business activities. The respondents stated they are not encouraging any specific product and that their instructions are to promote safe alternatives, including En-ripe, but they are not restricting or banning the petitioners' Ethephon product. The court ultimately found that the respondents did not interfere with the petitioners' business as long as the product is not banned and set aside the memo issued by respondent No. 2.

The petitioners claim that the state is interfering with their business despite Ethephon being approved by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI). The petitioners argue that both Ethephon and En-ripe (a product of respondent No. 3) are safe and approved for use, yet the state is favoring En-ripe over Ethephon. 4. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners argue that the state is unjustly discouraging the use of Ethephon, which is legally permitted. 2. The Government Pleader contends that Ethephon is toxic and poses health risks, thus justifying the promotion of safer alternatives. 3. The petitioners reference previous court rulings that support the use of both Ethephon and En-ripe. 

Court's reasoning: 1. The court reviewed the counter affidavit and found that the state did not recommend any specific product but aimed to inform farmers about safe ripening methods. 2. The court noted that FSSAI guidelines permit the use of Ethephon under certain conditions, including packaging requirements to prevent leakage. 3. The court concluded that the state authorities are not interfering with the petitioners' business as long as Ethephon is not banned. 

Decision or judgment: The court allowed the writ petition, setting aside the impugned memo dated 20-03-2020 issued by respondent No. 2. The court ruled that there would be no costs, and any pending miscellaneous applications were closed.

column3: The petitioners, M/S. Mokalbari Kanoi Tea Estate Pvt. Ltd. and another, exported their tea products to France. Some of these products were returned by the French buyers because they claimed the grades and qualities did not match their requirements. When the products returned to India, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) refused to give a no-objection for the petitioners to bring the products back into India, relying on visual inspection that indicated possible misrepresentation or misbranding due to conflicting information on the packaging about the "best before" date. The petitioners argued that the labels showing the "best before" date as June 2025 should prevail over pre-printed prints indicating a twelve-month shelf life from the manufacturing date, and that the authorities did not physically sample or examine the products to verify the actual remaining shelf life. The petitioners appealed, asserting that the refusal was invalid because no physical sampling or testing was conducted, and they requested an opportunity to produce evidence and have the products examined to confirm the true "best before" date. The court allowed the petitioners‚Äô challenge, set aside the refusals, and ordered the authorities to conduct sampling and examination before making a final decision.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a writ petition filed by M/S. Mokalbari Kanoi Tea Estate Pvt. Ltd. and another against the Union of India and other respondents regarding the refusal of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) to grant a no-objection for the importation of tea products that were returned from France due to quality issues. The petitioners challenge the FSSAI's decision based on alleged misbranding and misrepresentation of the 'best before' date on the products. Key facts: 1. The petitioners exported tea products to France, which were returned by the buyers due to non-compliance with their quality requirements. 2. The FSSAI refused to grant no-objection based on a visual inspection, claiming misrepresentation regarding the 'best before' date. 3. The packages indicated a 'best before' date of twelve months from the manufacturing date, while the petitioners' labels stated a date of June 2025. 4. The petitioners argue that the FSSAI did not provide sufficient evidence for their claims and did not conduct a proper examination of the products. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners contend that the FSSAI's refusal was arbitrary as it relied solely on visual inspection without sampling the products. 2. They cite Regulation 2(1)(c) of the Food Safety and Standards (Import) Regulations, 2017, and Regulation 2(1)(c) of the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020, to support their claims regarding the definition of 'best before' dates. 3. The respondents argue that the products did not meet the necessary shelf-life requirements as per Regulation 5(6) of the Import Regulations of 2017. 4. The respondents also refer to Section 3(zf)(i) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, regarding misbranding. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the FSSAI's rejection was based on the perception that the petitioners' labels were misleading, without proper examination of the products. 2. The court emphasized that there was no evidence of sampling or physical examination of the products to verify the claims made by the petitioners. 3. The court highlighted that the FSSAI should have provided the petitioners an opportunity to present their case and produce relevant documents. 4. The court concluded that the refusal by the FSSAI was vitiated due to lack of proper examination and consideration of the petitioners' claims. Decision or judgment: The court allowed W.P.A. No. 28958 of 2022, setting aside the FSSAI's refusal to grant no-objection for the importation of the products. The court directed the FSSAI to provide an opportunity for the petitioners to present their case and to conduct a physical examination of the products to ascertain the correct 'best before' date. The court ordered that this process be completed expeditiously, preferably within one month, and that the outcome be communicated to the petitioners. No order as to costs was made.

The respondent seized lighting oil from the petitioner's premises on April 20, 2020, but did not return it. The petitioner argued that the seized lighting oil is not food and thus the prosecution based on food safety laws is invalid. The petitioner had previously filed a court order to release the seized goods. The respondent clarified that the seized oil was lighting oil and not edible oil. The petitioner contended that lighting oil is not considered food according to the relevant legal definition and a circular issued by the Food Safety authority. The court found that the seized oil was lighting oil, not edible oil, and therefore the prosecution was not sustainable, leading to the quashing of the case.

A prior Writ Petition (W.P(MD)No.15211 of 2020) was filed to release the seized goods, and the court ordered the release of 188 oil tins on July 13, 2021. 3. The respondent's counsel confirmed that only lighting oil was seized, not edible oil. 3. The petitioner cites a circular from the Commissioner of Food Safety stating that lighting oil is not for edible use and should not be prosecuted under the Food Safety and Standards Act. The court noted that the seized oil was confirmed to be lighting oil, not edible oil, and therefore, the prosecution was not valid. 3. The court emphasized that the prosecution against the petitioner was unsustainable based on the nature of the seized product. column15:
Case overview
- The case is Britannia Industries Ltd vs Unknown, decided on 18 September 2024 by Hon'ble Pankaj Purohit, J. in the Uttarakhand High Court.
- The appeal was filed under Section 71(6) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 against a judgment from the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal, Kumaon Division, Haldwani, dated 20 July 2024.

Key facts
- The appellant, Britannia Industries Ltd, was fined ‚Çπ1,50,000 by the Adjudicating Officer in Adjudication Case No.51/66 of 2022 on 9 June 2023.
- The fine was imposed under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the appellant was required to deposit the amount within one month.
- The appellant filed an appeal (Misc. Appeal No.5 of 2023) against this order, but it was submitted after the 30-day limitation period as prescribed by Rule 3.3.1 of the Food Safety Rules, 2011.

Legal issues and arguments
- The appellant argued that the Appellate Tribunal incorrectly dismissed their application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which allows for the application of the Limitation Act to appeals unless otherwise stated in the Food Safety Act.
- The appellant contended that the Tribunal had the authority to condone the delay beyond the 30 days specified in the Food Safety Rules.
- The State's counsel argued that the Appellate Tribunal's power to extend the limitation period was limited to 30 days, and since the appeal was filed after 60 days, it was rightly dismissed as time barred.

Court's reasoning
- The Court noted that the Appellate Tribunal has the authority to condone delays only up to 30 days as per Rule 3.1 of the Food Safety Rules, 2011.
- The Court found that the Tribunal acted correctly in dismissing the appeal as it was filed beyond the permissible time limit.
- The Court rejected the appellant's argument that the Rules could not override the provisions of the Food Safety Act, stating that the Rules are made under the authority of the Act and do not contradict it.

Decision or judgment
- The High Court dismissed the appeal, affirming the Appellate Tribunal's decision to reject the appeal as time barred.

The authorities argued that the sampling and testing complied with procedures and that the reports indicated non-conformity with standards. The court was asked to consider whether the testing was valid and whether proceedings based on the reports were justified.

column15: Case overview: The case involves multiple writ petitions filed by M/s Pernod Ricard India Private Limited against the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and other respondents regarding adjudication proceedings for alleged contraventions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and related regulations. The petitions challenge the validity of the notice issued for adjudication based on the analysis of samples of alcoholic beverages. Key facts: 1. The petitioner is engaged in the manufacture, distribution, and sale of alcoholic beverages. 2. The petitioner received a notice of adjudication for contraventions of specific provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the Food Safety and Standards (Alcoholic Beverages) Regulations, 2018. 3. The petitioner contends that the samples were not tested by an accredited laboratory as required by law, as the laboratory's accreditation had expired prior to the analysis. 4. The respondents argue that the laboratory was accredited and that the sampling and analysis were conducted according to the prescribed procedures. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argues that the analysis report is invalid due to the lack of testing by an accredited laboratory, violating section 47 of the Act, 2006. 2. The petitioner claims that the Food Safety Officer failed to send a notice regarding the sampling, violating their right to have a fourth sample tested. 3. The respondents assert that the laboratory was accredited at the time of testing and that the sampling was conducted properly. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the laboratory that tested the samples did not have the appropriate scope of accreditation to analyze whisky, as per the regulations. 2. The court noted that the respondents could not demonstrate the laboratory's competence to test alcoholic beverages, which were outside the valid scope of recognition. 3. The court highlighted that the Executive Director of the Food Safety and Standards Authority had previously advised against sending samples to laboratories incapable of testing the product. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the writ petitions, ruling in favor of the petitioner and making the rule absolute in terms of the prayer clause, effectively invalidating the adjudication proceedings based on the flawed analysis.

column3: The case involves Satbir Singh, the food business operator at M/s Rewari Sweet Center in Nangal Raya, New Delhi, who was accused of storing and selling "Boondi Laddoo" that contained artificial colors exceeding permissible limits. The sample was prepared, divided into four parts, and preserved with formalin following proper procedures. One part was sent to the food analyst and another to a referral laboratory for testing. The analysis revealed that the food contained artificial colors, specifically tartrazine and sunset yellow, exceeding the maximum limit of 100 ppm, making it unsafe for human consumption. The accused pleaded not guilty, claimed the utensils used were not cleaned and dried properly, and argued that the sample collection process was flawed, alleging some yellow color was already present on utensils and in the bottles. The department argued that the sampling was proper, and the laboratory reports confirmed the artificial coloring was beyond permissible limits. The court considered the evidence and concluded that the food article was unsafe due to excessive artificial coloring, and the accused was convicted for selling unsafe food.

column15: Case overview: The case involves the prosecution of Satbir Singh, the proprietor of M/s Rewari Sweet Center, for selling unsafe food articles, specifically 'Boondi Laddoo', in violation of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The Food Safety Officer (FSO) conducted an inspection on October 18, 2014, leading to the collection of a sample that was later found to exceed permissible limits of synthetic coloring. The judgment was delivered on September 4, 2023, by ACMM Sh. Abhishek Kumar. Key facts: 1. The FSO, Bal Mukund, inspected the accused's shop and found 'Boondi Laddoo' stored without proper labeling. 2. A sample was purchased for analysis, which was later found to contain synthetic colors exceeding the legal limit. 3. The sample was analyzed by both a Food Analyst and a Referral Food Laboratory, both reporting the sample as unsafe. 4. The accused was given the opportunity to appeal the findings but was ultimately prosecuted. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The prosecution argued that the sample was collected according to the regulations and that the reports confirmed the presence of unsafe levels of synthetic coloring. 2. The defense contended that the sampling process was flawed, claiming the utensils used were not clean and dry, and that there were discrepancies between the two reports. 3. The defense cited various judgments to support their claims regarding the sampling process. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the prosecution had established its case beyond a reasonable doubt, confirming that the sample was unsafe for human consumption due to excessive synthetic coloring. 2. The court noted that the defense failed to provide credible evidence to support claims of improper sampling. 3. The court referenced a Supreme Court ruling that established the precedence of the Referral Food Laboratory's report over the Food Analyst's report once an appeal was made. Decision or judgment: The court convicted Satbir Singh for violating provisions of the FSS Act, specifically Section 26(2)(i) and Section 59(i), due to the sale of unsafe food. Sentencing was to be determined separately.

column3: The case involves Modicare Limited suing Maa Adishakti Multi Trade Enterprises and associated defendants for infringing on its 'WELL' series of trademarks and product labels used for health, nutrition, and wellness products. Modicare Limited is a company that manufactures, markets, and sells FMCG products, including food, personal care, and health products, through a network of consultants, support centers, and SKUs. It claims rights to various 'WELL' marks registered since 2002 and 2012, and asserts that it has built goodwill through long and continuous use, supported by certifications and licenses from agencies like USDANOP, Naturland Organic, Ecocert, and FSSAI. The plaintiff alleges that the defendants marketed products with names such as 'WELL INTELLECTE,' 'WELL KOREAN RED GINSENG,' 'WELL D-TOX,' 'WELL JOINT EASE,' 'WELL AM-PM,' and 'WELL NATUROPAUSE,' which are identical or deceptively similar to its marks, labels, and trade dress. The plaintiff discovered in July 2019 that the defendants were selling infringing products online via platforms such as Amazon, Shopclues, and Snapdeal, often using fake licenses and fake product labels that mimic the plaintiff's design and branding to create confusion. The defendants' online listings, website, and product labels were found to be identical or similar to the plaintiff‚Äôs, and evidence suggests they were connected and jointly involved in selling the infringing products. The plaintiff sought and obtained an interim order restraining the defendants from manufacturing or selling infringing products. Despite being served, the defendants did not file any defense or appearance. The court found that the defendant‚Äôs product names and labels had been copied and registered in the plaintiff‚Äôs favor, and that their activity was likely to cause consumer confusion and pass-off. The court also noted the likelihood of confusion between the infringing and original products, particularly given their similarity in name, packaging, and category of health-related products, which are treated with a high degree of vigilance to prevent consumer deception. Based on these facts, the court granted a permanent injunction restraining the defendants from manufacturing, selling, or using infringing marks and labels, and ordered the delisting of their products from online platforms, along with costs awarded to the plaintiff.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a suit filed by Modicare Limited against Maa Adishakti Multi Trade Enterprises and three other defendants for trademark infringement and passing off related to the use of the mark 'WELL' and its variants in the marketing of health and wellness products. The suit was heard by Justice Prathiba M. Singh in the High Court of Delhi on October 13, 2023. Key facts: 1. Modicare Limited is a direct selling company part of the K.K. Modi Group, selling FMCG products including health and wellness items. 2. The Plaintiff claims rights to the 'WELL' mark since 2004 and has multiple registered trademarks related to it. 3. The Plaintiff's products have significant sales figures, exceeding Rs. 212 crores in 2018-2019, and are certified by various agencies. 4. The Defendants are accused of using similar marks such as 'WELL INTELLECTE' and 'WELL D-TOX', which the Plaintiff claims are identical to its registered marks. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The Plaintiff alleges that the Defendants' use of similar marks constitutes trademark infringement and passing off, leading to consumer confusion. 2. The Plaintiff sought an interim injunction against the Defendants to prevent them from using the infringing marks. 3. The Defendants did not appear in court or file a written statement, leading to a request for summary judgment by the Plaintiff. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the Defendants had been repeatedly served and had failed to defend the case, justifying the grant of summary judgment. 2. The court emphasized the importance of preventing consumer confusion in the health and wellness sector, applying stricter standards for nutraceutical products akin to pharmaceuticals. 3. The court found that the Defendants' actions were likely to mislead consumers and infringe upon the Plaintiff's trademarks. Decision or judgment: The court granted a permanent injunction against the Defendants, restraining them from manufacturing or selling products under the 'WELL' marks or any deceptively similar variants. The Defendants were ordered to remove their infringing products from online platforms within two weeks. The Plaintiff was awarded costs amounting to Rs. 11,63,650, and the suit was decreed in favor of the Plaintiff.

column3: V. Ramesh and others were accused in a case involving the handling of a food sample. The complaint was filed by the Food Safety Officer, representing the Tamil Nadu Food Safety Department, against the petitioners for offences under section 59(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The food sample was received by the food analyst on January 29, 2019, but the report was only sent on March 12, 2019, beyond the required 14-day period, with reasons for the delay provided only on that date. The petitioners argued that this delay violated legal provisions, specifically section 42(2) of the Act, and therefore the complaint should be quashed. The respondent's side contended that the delay was explained and no prejudice was caused. The court found that the sample analysis report was delayed and the reasons for delay were not provided within the statutory timeframe, thus violating the law, leading to the quashing of the complaint.

Case overview
- The case is titled Crl.Rev.P./16/2024 and was heard in the Gauhati High Court. 
- The petitioner is Abhijit Saikai, a practicing advocate and manager of Eden Cold Storage. 
- The respondent is the State of Assam, represented by the Public Prosecutor. 
- The judgment was delivered by Hon'ble Mrs. Justice Mitali Thakuria on 20 March 2024.

Key facts
- On 29 November 2023, a refrigerated van carrying packaged buffalo meat was intercepted by police at Srirampur gate. 
- The vehicle was seized along with two mobile phones and a chamber of the cold storage. 
- The petitioner applied for the return (Zimma) of the vehicle and items, which was denied by the lower court due to failure to provide a bank guarantee as required under Section 11(5) of the Assam Cattle Preservation Act.
- The petitioner argued that the seizure was illegal as the vehicle was not carrying live cattle and that the police had no jurisdiction to seize the mobile phones and cold storage.

Legal issues and arguments
- The petitioner contended that the Assam Cattle Preservation Act applies only to live cattle and slaughter, not to processed meat. 
- The petitioner claimed that the cold storage is registered under the FSSAI Act, and only food safety officers have the authority to take samples, not the police. 
- The petitioner cited Section 102 of the Cr.P.C, arguing that police cannot seize immovable property.
- The respondent argued that the mobile phones and cold storage were necessary for further investigation, as the FSL report indicated the presence of cow antigen in the samples sent for examination.

Court's reasoning
- The court noted that the vehicle was carrying processed meat, which was claimed to be buffalo meat but tested positive for beef, thus falling under the purview of the Assam Cattle Preservation Act. 
- The court referenced the Supreme Court's ruling that police do not have the authority to seize immovable property under Section 102 of the Cr.P.C. 
- The court acknowledged the need for the cold storage and mobile phones for ongoing investigations but found the sealing of the cold storage unjustified under the law.

Decision or judgment
- The court disposed of the criminal revision petition, allowing the petitioner to approach the lower court for unsealing the cold storage. 
- The court upheld the rejection of the zimma for the mobile phones, citing concerns over potential tampering and the need for further investigation. 
- The petitioner may apply for the release of the vehicle, which the lower court will consider in accordance with the Assam Cattle Preservation Act.

- The applicant, Dayal Khoobchandani, is challenging an order dated 19 June 2019 from the 9th Additional District Judge, Satna, which affirmed a penalty imposed by the Judgmental Officer cum Additional District Magistrate, Satna, on 25 April 2017.

- The civil revision was dismissed, with no order as to costs. Any pending miscellaneous applications were also closed.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a complaint filed by the Food Safety Officer against Vivekanand Parikh, Kishan Kumar, and M/s Bikaner Namkeen Bhandar for violations under Section 26/59 of the Food Safety & Standards Act, 2006. The complaint arose from an inspection conducted on October 20, 2013, where unsafe food articles were found for sale. The court delivered its judgment on December 14, 2023, acquitting all accused. Key facts: 1. The Food Safety Officer inspected M/s Bikaner Namkeen Bhandar and collected a sample of 'Ras Madhuri' for analysis. 2. The sample was found to contain excessive synthetic dye, exceeding the permissible limit. 3. The accused did not appeal the Food Analyst's report. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The prosecution argued that the sample was unsafe due to excessive dye content. 2. The defense challenged the validity of the sanction for prosecution and the admissibility of the Food Analyst's report, claiming the lab lacked the accreditation for quantitative analysis. 3. The defense also argued that one accused was not properly served with the report, violating their right to appeal. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the sanction for prosecution was valid, as the acting Commissioner had the authority to grant it. 2. The court noted that the lab's report was questionable due to the lack of accreditation for quantitative analysis, raising doubts about the prosecution's case. 3. The court acknowledged that one accused was not served the report, which prejudiced their defense. Decision or judgment: The court acquitted all accused persons of the charges under Section 59(i) of the FSS Act, 2006, concluding that the prosecution failed to establish the case beyond reasonable doubt.

The case pertains to allegations of food adulteration under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Key facts: 1. The sample in question was a laddu, which was alleged to contain a non-permitted coloring agent. 2. The sample was collected on February 20, 2013, and the analyst report was received on March 6, 2013. 3. A complaint case was lodged on July 26, 2013. 4. The cognizance was taken under section 3(zz) and section 59(ii) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argues that the cognizance taken is not in accordance with law, claiming that section 59(ii) pertains to grievous injury, which is not applicable in this case. 2. The petitioner contends that the definition section (section 3(zz)) was improperly used to take cognizance, indicating a lack of judicial application. 3. The respondent State's counsel asserts that the sample was found to be adulterated, justifying the complaint. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the only allegation was regarding the use of non-permitted color in the laddu, and there were no further allegations of grievous injury. 2. The court noted that the use of section 59(ii) was inappropriate as it did not apply to the circumstances of the case. 3. The court concluded that the cognizance taken was flawed due to the non-application of judicial mind. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the petition and quashed the entire criminal proceeding, including the order taking cognizance dated August 2, 2013, in C.G.Case No.4 of 2013. A notice was issued demanding that devotees obtain permission to offer Annathanam, which prompted the petitioner to send a representation on May 1, 2023, requesting the withdrawal of the notice. 3. The petitioner filed the writ petition after receiving no response from the respondents. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argued that the notice was unnecessary and sought its withdrawal. 2. The respondents clarified that the notice was a public awareness initiative and not directed at any individual, and no strict action would be taken against violations for that year. Court's reasoning: 1. The Designated Officer stated that the notice was intended to create awareness about the licensing requirement for future festivals. 2. The court noted that since the festival had progressed and the arrangements for Annathanam had already been made, no further orders were necessary. Decision or judgment: The court closed the writ petition, directing the respondents to create awareness among devotees regarding the licensing requirement for future Chitirai Festivals. No costs were awarded, and the connected miscellaneous petition was also closed.

- The case is titled Cannaught Plaza Restaurant Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of Punjab and Another, decided on 30 April 2024 by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana. 
- The petitioner is Cannaught Plaza Restaurant Private Limited, and the respondents are the State of Punjab and another party.

Key facts
- The petitioner sought to set aside an order dated 12 October 2022 from the Court of Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Jalandhar, which declared the petitioner a proclaimed person in a case arising from complaint COMA No. 630 of 2015 under Sections 26 and 27 of the Food Safety & Standards Act, 2006.
- The petitioner argued that it was not properly impleaded in the complaint, as it was named as Mcdonalds (Restaurant) Axis Building, BMC Square Jalandhar through its Managing Director.
- The petitioner indicated readiness to join the proceedings in the trial court to expedite the trial.

Legal issues and arguments
- The petitioner contended that the impugned order was unsustainable due to improper impleadment in the complaint.
- The petitioner referenced a resolution dated 4 March 2024 to support its claim of being a distinct entity from the one named in the complaint.
- The respondent's counsel, Mr. J.S. Dhaliwal, AAG Punjab, argued that the trial court's order was lawful under Section 82 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).

Court's reasoning
- The court noted that the petitioner was indeed running its business under a different name than that used in the complaint.
- The court did not express an opinion on the merits of the case but found grounds to set aside the impugned order based on the improper naming of the petitioner.

Decision or judgment
- The High Court set aside the impugned order and directed the petitioner to appear before the trial court within 15 days to seek bail.
- The petitioner was ordered to pay costs of Rs. 7500 to the District Legal Services Authority concerned.

column15: Case overview: The case involves multiple writ petitions filed by M/S Surendra Associates and other theatre owners against the Entertainment Tax Officer and the Government of Andhra Pradesh regarding the validity of G.O.Ms.No.100, which revised ticket prices for cinema theatres. The petitioners challenge the government's decision to maintain lower ticket prices for air-conditioned theatres compared to non-air-conditioned theatres, which they argue is discriminatory and contrary to the recommendations of a High Power Committee. Key facts: 1. The earlier G.O.Ms.No.181 was struck down by the court, leading to the formation of a High Power Committee to recommend ticket pricing. 2. The committee suggested a maximum ticket price of Rs.75 for the highest class and Rs.20 for the lowest class, but the government maintained the lowest price at Rs.10 for air-conditioned theatres and Rs.6 for non-air-conditioned theatres. 3. The petitioners argue that this creates an unfair situation where non-air-conditioned theatres are allowed to charge the same minimum price as air-conditioned theatres. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners contend that the government's decision deviates from the committee's recommendations and violates the A.P. Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1955. 2. The government argues that the recommendations are advisory and that the fixed rates aim to benefit poorer cine-goers. 3. The petitioners seek to have the G.O. set aside and to be allowed to charge ticket prices as per the committee's recommendations. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the G.O. was issued following the directions of the court in a previous case and that the committee's recommendations were not binding. 2. The court acknowledged the changed circumstances since the G.O. was issued, including the conversion of some theatres into multiplexes with advanced infrastructure. 3. The court found that the G.O. was not proportionate to the current situation and warranted revision. Decision or judgment: The court set aside G.O.Ms.No.100 and directed both governments to form respective committees to review ticket pricing, ensuring the welfare of cine-goers and addressing the grievances of exhibitors. The petitioners were permitted to collect their proposed ticket fares while informing the authorities of the rates. The court also directed that taxes be paid proportionate to the proposed ticket rates.
