Case overview
- The case is titled Awadhesh @ Kallu Sharma vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh, heard in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Gwalior on May 20, 2024.
- The applicant is Awadhesh @ Kallu Sharma, a 40-year-old resident of Gohad Chauraha, District Bhind, Madhya Pradesh.
- The respondent is the State of Madhya Pradesh, represented by the Station Police Station Gohad Chauraha.

Key facts
- The applicant filed a first application for anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Cr.P.C. concerning FIR No.306 of 2023.
- The FIR alleges offences under Sections 420, 272, and 273 of the IPC.
- The allegations stem from an inspection on November 3, 2023, by Food Safety Officer Avinash Gupta, where the applicant was found selling materials used for preparing adulterated milk.
- Seven samples of the adulterated substance were taken, and the shop was sealed.

Legal issues and arguments
- The applicant's counsel argued that the applicant is innocent and has been falsely implicated, asserting that no food material was found in the shop.
- It was contended that the FIR is illegal as it is based solely on the allegation of selling dairy-related equipment.
- The counsel highlighted that under Section 42(3) of The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, prior sanction from the Commissioner is required for prosecution, which was not obtained.
- It was further argued that if the sample is found to be sub-standard, only penalties can be imposed under Sections 51 & 57 of The Food Safety and Standards Act, and no imprisonment is provided for such offences.
- The applicant's counsel cited decisions from the Supreme Court in Ram Nath Vs. The State of U.P. and Sushil Kumar Gupta Vs. State of West Bengal to support the arguments.
- The applicant is a permanent resident of District Bhind, and there is no risk of absconding or tampering with evidence.

Court's reasoning
- The court considered the arguments from both parties and reviewed the case diary.
- Without expressing an opinion on the merits of the case, the court found sufficient grounds to grant anticipatory bail.

Decision or judgment
- The application for anticipatory bail was allowed.
- The applicant is to be released on bail upon executing a personal bond of Rs.1,00,000 with one solvent surety of the same amount to the satisfaction of the Arresting Officer/Investigating Authority.
- The applicant must comply with the conditions under Section 438(2) of the Cr.P.C. and cooperate with the investigation; failure to do so will result in automatic cancellation of the bail order.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a writ petition filed by M/S ITC Limited against the Food Safety Inspector and the Designated Officer of the Department of Food Safety and Standards, challenging an order dated December 29, 2015, which imposed a fine for misbranding of their product, Sunfeast Yippee Noodles. The petition was heard in the High Court of Karnataka, Kalaburagi Bench. Key facts: 1. The petitioner, M/S ITC Limited, manufactures instant noodles and was accused of misbranding due to the label stating 'No Added MSG'. 2. A sample was collected on June 8, 2015, and tested, with the Chief Food Analyst reporting it as misbranded. 3. The petitioner claimed they were not given proper notice or the right to appeal against the Food Analyst's report. 4. The Designated Officer imposed a fine of Rs. 10,000 based on the Food Analyst's report. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argued that the product complied with all standards and that the misbranding claim was unfounded, as there was no evidence that MSG was added during manufacturing. 2. They contended that the prosecution was initiated without proper inspection of the manufacturing premises and without affording them the right to appeal as per Section 46(4) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. 3. The respondents maintained that the product was misbranded due to the label claim and that the prosecution was justified. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the Chief Food Analyst's report indicated compliance with standards but also stated that the product was misbranded due to the label claim. 2. It highlighted that there was no analytical method to determine if MSG was added or naturally present, and that prosecution should not occur without ascertaining the addition of MSG during manufacturing. 3. The court found that the Designated Officer did not inspect the manufacturing unit, which was necessary to determine the validity of the misbranding claim. 4. The court emphasized that the petitioner was not given the opportunity to appeal, violating principles of natural justice. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the writ petition, quashing the order passed by the Additional District Magistrate cum Adjudicating Authority in C.C.No.316/203/54/2015-16 dated December 29, 2015, against M/S ITC Limited.

The petitioners contended that these conditions were onerous and tailored to favor certain large applicants, thus depriving small and medium poultry farmers of fair opportunity. They further argued that the change from project-wise tenders to zonal tenders adversely affected their interests. The respondents maintained that the tender conditions aimed to ensure quality eggs supply for children's nutrition programs, in line with government policies, and that the conditions such as "Agmark" certification and financial turnover are justified to maintain quality standards. The petitioners also sought to include representations made via email, which were ignored by the respondents, challenging the legality of not considering their input. The respondents contended that the tender process and conditions were lawful, rational, and aligned with public health and nutrition objectives, and that the petitioners' participation was disqualified due to their failure to qualify in the technical bid.

- The writ petition was allowed and disposed of.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a Criminal Misc. Application No. 2447 of 2019 filed by Neeraj Nainwal against the State of Uttarakhand regarding the cognizance of an offence under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The applicant challenges the order dated 29.04.2019 by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Nainital, which took cognizance of the offence and rejected the applicant's discharge. The case number is 597 of 2018, State Vs. Neeraj Nainwal. Key facts: 1. The cognizance order was issued on 23rd October 2017, which the applicant claims violates the provisions of Section 77 of the Act. 2. Section 77 states that no court shall take cognizance of an offence after one year from the date of commission unless the Commissioner of Food Safety assigns reasons for an extension up to three years. 3. The applicant argues that the cognizance order did not contain any reasons for the extension. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The applicant contends that the cognizance order is invalid due to the lack of reasons provided by the Food Safety Commissioner for extending the prosecution period. 2. The applicant also challenges the dismissal of his discharge application, asserting that the initial cognizance order was flawed. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the cognizance order dated 23rd October 2017 was indeed in violation of the proviso to Section 77, as it lacked the necessary reasons for extending the prosecution period. 2. The court concluded that since the cognizance order was invalid, the subsequent rejection of the discharge application was also invalid. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the C482 Application, quashing the order of rejection of discharge and the cognizance order, thereby nullifying the proceedings in Criminal Case No. 597 of 2018, State Vs. Neeraj Nainwal.

Case overview
- The case is titled Deendayal Somani S/O Banshilal Somani vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, heard in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh on August 9, 2024.
- The applicant, Deendayal Somani, is the proprietor of M/s Shri Nakodasaales.

Key facts
- The applicant filed a petition under section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) seeking to set aside various orders related to a criminal case concerning food safety.
- The sample in question was taken by a Food Safety Officer on September 14, 2011, and the complaint was filed on November 18, 2014, more than three years after the alleged offence.
- The applicant argued that the complaint was filed beyond the one-year limitation period prescribed by section 77 of the Food Safety & Standards Act, 2006.

Legal issues and arguments
- The applicant contended that according to section 77 of the Food Safety & Standards Act, cognizance of an offence must be taken within one year from the date of the offence, with a possible extension up to three years only if approved by the Commissioner of Food Safety.
- The applicant's counsel cited several legal precedents to support the argument that the prosecution was barred by limitation due to the delay in filing the complaint.
- The State opposed the applicant's prayer, but did not provide substantial counterarguments regarding the limitation issue.

Court's reasoning
- The court emphasized that the limitation period must be counted from the date of the offence, not from the date of the report or sanction for prosecution.
- The court referenced the Supreme Court ruling in State of Punjab vs Sarwan Singh, which highlighted the importance of limitation periods to prevent the loss of evidence and to avoid vexatious prosecutions.
- The court found that the complaint was indeed filed after the limitation period had expired, thus rendering the prosecution invalid.

Decision or judgment
- The High Court allowed the petition, set aside the orders dated January 18, 2021, and October 1, 2021, and discharged the applicant from the charges against him.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a revision petition filed by Nagendra Singh and M/s Thea Kitchen Private Limited against the summoning order dated January 18, 2021, issued by the Ld. ACMM-01, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi, concerning alleged violations of food safety regulations. The decision was rendered on April 17, 2023. Key facts: 1. The sample in question was taken on June 11, 2019. 2. The complaint alleges that the accused added synthetic color Tartrazine yellow to a food product, violating specific provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and related regulations. 3. The complaint cites violations of Section 26(1), Section 26(2)(i), and Section 27 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, as well as Regulation 3.1.2(1) and 3.1.2(6) of The Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additive) Regulations, 2011. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The accused's counsel argued that the cited regulations had been amended and omitted as of September 8, 2016, which should affect the summoning order. 2. The Ld. Magistrate's summoning order did not address the implications of the amendment or any potential mistakes in the complaint. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the Ld. Magistrate failed to consider the effect of the amendment on the case. 2. The court emphasized the need for the Ld. Magistrate to interpret the amended provisions and their relevance to the case. 3. The summoning order was deemed unsustainable due to the lack of consideration of the legal changes. Decision or judgment: The court set aside the summoning order and directed the lower court to hear the prosecution afresh, taking into account the changes in law post-amendment of 2016. The parties were ordered to appear before the concerned court on May 24, 2023.

column3: The petitioner, Vineet Goyal, faced trial under various sections related to food safety violations after wheat was found to be adulterated by artificial shining and coloring during an inspection on December 3, 2020. The wheat was packed and intended for sale in different districts of Madhya Pradesh and other states. The inspection team also found 40 kg of saffron-colored solution and 1 kg of non-edible saffron color. Samples of food grains and other articles were sent to the food testing laboratory, which confirmed the use of coloring agents. The petitioner challenged a penalty order of one lakh rupees imposed on him and sought to have the Food Analyst examined as a defense witness. The adjudicating authority rejected this application without explanation. The petitioner argued that the authority had the power to summon experts and that his right to produce relevant evidence was violated. The respondent's case was based on the inspection findings, the test reports, and the shipment of adulterated wheat for sale. The court ultimately found that the adjudicating authority's failure to consider the petitioner‚Äôs request to examine the Food Analyst was incorrect, and directed the authority to allow the petitioner to summon the Food Analyst for cross-examination.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a writ petition filed by Vineet Goyal against the State of Madhya Pradesh challenging an order dated January 30, 2023, from the Adjudicating Authority under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which rejected his application to summon the Food Analyst as a defense witness. The petitioner is facing trial under various sections of the Act of 2006 and had previously been penalized with a fine of Rs. 1.00 Lakh, which was later set aside by the Appellate Tribunal. Key facts: 1. The petitioner was found to have adulterated wheat during an inspection on December 3, 2020, where artificial coloring was used. 2. Samples were sent to the State Food Testing Laboratory, which confirmed the adulteration. 3. The petitioner sought to summon the Food Analyst for cross-examination after the Food Safety Officer was examined. 4. The Adjudicating Authority dismissed the application without providing reasons. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argued that he has a statutory right to summon the Food Analyst to defend himself against the allegations. 2. The respondent contended that the petitioner has no right to summon an expert and that the Adjudicating Authority's decision should stand. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that under Section 293 of the Cr.P.C., an expert can be summoned to provide evidence regarding their report. 2. The court emphasized that the Adjudicating Authority failed to exercise its jurisdiction by not allowing the petitioner to summon the Food Analyst. 3. The court highlighted the importance of providing the petitioner an opportunity to defend himself adequately. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the writ petition, set aside the impugned order dated January 30, 2023, and directed the Adjudicating Authority to permit the petitioner to summon the Food Analyst for cross-examination.

column3: The case involves Diamond Beverages Private Limited and a Food Safety Officer. The incident began on February 18, 2017, when packaged drinking water intended for human consumption was seized and sent for chemical testing due to suspicion of misbranding. The adjudicating authority examined the case and dismissed the misbranding allegation but ordered the company to include the names of sodium salts on the label within one month to comply with labeling regulations. The appellant challenged this order, arguing that the adjudicating officer exceeded their authority by issuing an improvement notice, which should have been issued by a designated officer under the law. The appellant contended that the order was illegal because it was issued without proper jurisdiction. The court considered whether the adjudicating officer could exercise the powers of the designated officer and found that they could not, as the powers were distinct. The appellant argued that the adjudicating officer's order was thus invalid, and the court admitted the appeal, staying the execution of the original order for ten weeks.

column15: Case overview: The case involves an appeal filed by Diamond Beverages Private Limited against the Food Safety Officer under Section 71(6) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, challenging an order from the Appellate Tribunal that dismissed their appeal regarding an advisory order from the adjudicating authority. The advisory order required the company to disclose the names of salts of sodium on their product label, following the seizure of their packaged drinking water on February 18, 2017, for alleged misbranding. Key facts: 1. The packaged drinking water was seized and sent for chemical examination due to concerns of misbranding under Section 3(1)(zf) of the Food Safety and Standards Act. 2. The adjudicating authority ruled out the misbranding allegation but issued an advisory order for labeling compliance under Regulation 2.2.2.2 (c) of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labeling) Regulations, 2011. 3. The Appellate Tribunal upheld the adjudicating authority's order, stating it was merely an improvement direction under Section 32 of the Act. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The appellant contended that the adjudicating officer overstepped their jurisdiction by issuing an improvement order, which should only be within the powers of a designated officer as defined in the Act. 2. The appellant argued that the powers of the adjudicating officer, as outlined in Section 68, do not include the authority to issue improvement orders under Section 32. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that a prima facie case was established by the appellant regarding the jurisdictional issue raised. 2. The court noted that the powers of the adjudicating officer are distinct from those of the designated officer, and the adjudicating officer cannot usurp the powers of the designated officer to issue improvement orders. Decision or judgment: The appeal was admitted, and the operation of the order dated November 12, 2021, passed by the adjudicating officer was stayed for ten weeks or until further orders. The appellant was directed to serve a copy of the application to the respondent and file an affidavit of service on the returnable date.

column15:
Case overview
- Case Number: 19901-2016
- Complainant: Food Safety Officer, Department of Food Safety
- Accused: Amit Kumar and Rajiv Brijwasi
- Offence Charged: Section 59 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act, 2006)
- Date of Judgment: 26 April 2024
- Final Judgment: Accused persons acquitted.

Key facts
- The complaint was filed on 09 May 2014.
- On 05 October 2013, a Food Safety Officer (FSO) inspected the shop "Shree Bankey Bihari Rasgulle" where Amit Kumar was found selling "Yellow Cham Cham" without proper labeling.
- The FSO collected a sample of the food item for analysis, which was later found to contain synthetic dye above permissible limits.
- The Food Analyst reported the sample as unsafe due to excessive artificial coloring (Taratazine) at 122.56 ppm.
- The accused were given an opportunity to appeal against the Food Analyst's report but did not do so.

Legal issues and arguments
- The prosecution argued that the accused violated the FSS Act by selling unsafe food.
- The defense contended that the sample collection was not conducted according to regulations and raised doubts about the Food Analyst's report, including the delay in report preparation and lack of specific testing methods.
- The defense also argued that the accused were not properly notified of the Food Analyst's report, violating their rights under Section 46(4) of the FSS Act.

Court's reasoning
- The court found that the prosecution failed to establish the case beyond a reasonable doubt.
- It noted that the sample collection was conducted according to the rules, and the defense did not provide credible evidence to counter the prosecution's claims.
- However, the court highlighted significant procedural lapses, including the failure to properly notify the accused of the Food Analyst's report, which undermined the prosecution's case.
- The court emphasized that any doubt in the case must be resolved in favor of the accused.

Decision or judgment
- The court acquitted both accused persons, Amit Kumar and Rajiv Brijwasi, of the charges under Section 59 of the FSS Act, 2006.
- The accused were directed to furnish personal bonds under Section 437A of the CrPC in the sum of Rs. 10,000 each.

The petitioner disputes the FIR's validity, arguing that proceedings under the Food Safety Act have already been initiated and that the FIR relates to different offenses. The respondents contend that the petitioner knowingly sold adulterated Ghee and that the offenses under IPC are separate from those under the Food Safety Act.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a criminal miscellaneous petition filed by Rajkumar against the State of Rajasthan seeking to quash FIR No.0424/2017, which was registered for offenses under Sections 420, 272, 103, and 104 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The petitioner argues that the FIR does not disclose any offense against him as he was unaware that the Ghee he sold was substandard and misbranded. Key facts: 1. The FIR was registered on August 10, 2017, at Police Station Suratgarh, District Sri Ganganagar. 2. The petitioner claims he purchased the Ghee from a manufacturer and was not the manufacturer of the substandard product. 3. Complaints were filed against the petitioner based on the report of the Food Safety Officer, and he was fined in those complaints. 4. The petitioner contends that the proceedings under the Food Safety Act have already been initiated and concluded, making the FIR redundant. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argues that the FIR should be quashed as it does not establish any offense against him. 2. The Public Prosecutor opposes the petition, asserting that the petitioner, in connivance with another accused, sold misbranded and adulterated Ghee under fake brands. 3. The prosecution argues that the offenses under IPC are distinct from those under the Food Safety and Standards Act. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the police investigation revealed a significant quantity of adulterated Ghee sold under fake brands, implicating the petitioner. 2. The court emphasized that the petitioner‚Äôs prior punishment by the Food Safety Officer does not justify quashing the FIR. 3. The court concluded that the actions of the petitioner fall within the ambit of IPC offenses, as he knowingly sold adulterated Ghee. Decision or judgment: The court dismissed the criminal miscellaneous petition filed by the petitioner under Section 482 Cr.P.C, affirming the validity of the FIR and allowing the proceedings to continue. All pending applications were also dismissed.

column15: Case overview: The case involves a writ petition filed by M/s. Sri Sai Krishna Kalyana Mandapam against the Commissioner of Food Safety and other respondents, challenging the legality of a notice issued under Section 31(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which directed the petitioner to register and obtain a license for operating a marriage hall. The petition was heard by Justice M. Dhandapani in the High Court of Judicature at Madras on June 20, 2023. Key facts: 1. The petitioner operates a marriage hall and rents it out for functions, receiving rent from customers. 2. The respondents issued notices to the petitioner, claiming that the marriage hall has a kitchen and requires a license under the Food Safety Act. 3. The petitioner contends that they do not prepare food and that customers hire their own cooks or caterers. 4. The petitioner filed an affidavit stating that they do not engage in food preparation or storage. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argues that the notice is illegal and without jurisdiction, as they do not prepare or sell food. 2. The respondents argue that the presence of a kitchen in the marriage hall necessitates a license under the Food Safety Act, regardless of who prepares the food. 3. The respondents cite concerns regarding food safety and hygiene at events held in the marriage hall. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the petitioner claims to rent the hall and does not engage in food preparation or distribution. 2. The court found that the notice issued by the third respondent was not sustainable, as the petitioner was not involved in food manufacturing or supply. 3. The court acknowledged that if the respondents later determine that the petitioner is involved in food preparation, they may take appropriate action. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the writ petition, set aside the notice issued by the third respondent, and stated that this order does not prevent the respondents from taking action if they find evidence of food preparation by the petitioner in the future. No costs were awarded, and the connected miscellaneous petition was closed.

- The petitioner submitted an e-tender for the supply of food grains, vegetables, sanitation, stationary, building construction materials, and other materials for Central Jail and District Jail in Indore for the financial year 2023-2024.

- The petitioner argued that they complied with condition no. 10 (viii) by submitting the license.

- The respondents maintained that the incomplete submission led to the rejection of the tender as it did not meet the specified requirements.

Court's reasoning
- The court noted that the petitioner failed to provide a complete copy of the license as required by the tender conditions.
- It emphasized that the term 'license' in the context of the tender must be interpreted to mean a complete document, not just a part of it.
- The court found that the petitioner did not rectify the incomplete submission even after the respondents filed their replies, leading to an adverse inference against the petitioner.
- The court stated that in contractual matters, the terms and conditions of the tender must be interpreted strictly.

Decision or judgment
- The High Court dismissed the writ petition, concluding that there was no case for interference under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

column3: The petitioner, Ins Consultancy through its proprietor, imported roasted areca nuts (split). The case involves a dispute over whether the imported nuts conform to safety and quality standards. The petitioner argued that the nuts meet the requirements of the relevant food safety regulations. The Customs Department, represented by Deputy Commissioner Shweta Suman, relied on a report from an accredited laboratory that suggested the nuts were not fully roasted. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), through its Deputy Director, issued an affidavit stating that the nuts conformed to the required standards and that they had no objection to clearance. There was conflicting information between the FSSAI's report and the laboratory report from the NABL-accredited lab, which took a contrary view about the roasting of the nuts. The court directed that the nuts be sampled again and tested by a third accredited laboratory, with the results to determine if the nuts were fit for human consumption and properly roasted. Both parties agreed to accept the final test report, and if favorable, the goods would be released upon the petitioner executing a bond. The case was adjourned to a later date for further proceedings based on the new report.

column3: The petitioners, including Nomula Poultry Farm and six other small poultry farmers, challenged a tender issued on November 21, 2022, by the Women Development & Child Welfare Department of Telangana for the procurement of eggs under a zonal system, which replaced the existing project-based system. The tender required bidders to have specific qualifications, including "Agmark" certification, ISO certification, FSSAI license, and a turnover of at least Rs. 5 crores in any one of the last three years, as well as experience in supplying eggs worth at least Rs. 5 crores in a year. The petitioners argued that these conditions favored large players and excluded small farmers, depriving them of participation. They also contended that the conditions related to certification and turnover were onerous and unfeasible within the time provided, and that the change to the zonal tender system disadvantaged small poultry farmers. The petitioners further claimed that the tender conditions appeared tailored to benefit certain pre-selected bidders and that the changes were made without proper consultation, in violation of existing schemes and guidelines. Meanwhile, other petitioners in related cases sought to have their email representations considered and to be declared qualified for the tender, but their bids were ultimately rejected in the technical evaluation. The respondents maintained that the tender conditions aimed to ensure quality and safety standards for eggs supplied to beneficiaries under the ICDS scheme and that the tender process was fair, legal, and in accordance with government policies and previous rulings. The court ultimately dismissed the petitions, holding that the conditions were lawful, non-discriminatory, and in public interest, and that participation in the tender was not a right but a privilege, subject to the criteria set by the authorities.

Case overview: The case involves three writ petitions filed by Nomula Poultry Farm and others against the State of Telangana regarding Tender Reference No.3347/SNP/2022 issued by the Women Development and Child Welfare Department for the procurement and supply of eggs under the Arogyalakshmi and supplementary nutrition programme. The petitioners challenge the tender conditions, claiming they are arbitrary and detrimental to small poultry farmers. The petitions were heard together due to common questions of fact and law. 

Key facts: 1. The tender was issued on November 21, 2022, for a two-year period (January 2023 - December 2024) for supplying eggs to beneficiaries. 2. The tender includes a zonal system for procurement, allowing bidders to bid for a maximum of two zones. 3. The qualifying conditions include requirements for Agmark certification, ISO certification, and a minimum turnover of Rs.5 crores in the last three years. 4. The petitioners argue that these conditions are designed to exclude small farmers. 

Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners argue that the tender conditions are unreasonable and tailored to benefit certain applicants, thus violating Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. 2. They claim the conditions were not discussed with poultry farmers and that the requirement for Agmark certification is impractical. 3. The respondents argue that the conditions are necessary to ensure quality and safety in the supply of eggs and that the tender process is transparent and open to multiple bidders. 

Court's reasoning: 1. The court emphasized the limited scope of judicial review in tender matters, stating it would not interfere unless the conditions were found to be arbitrary or irrational. 2. The court found that the conditions were justified in light of the need for quality assurance in the supply of eggs. 3. The court noted that the petitioners had not established any mala fides or arbitrary intent behind the tender conditions. 4. The court concluded that the inclusion of Agmark certification and the turnover requirement were reasonable and in the public interest. 

Decision or judgment: The court dismissed all three writ petitions, upholding the validity of the tender conditions and stating that the petitioners, having participated in the tender process and not qualified in the technical bid, could not challenge the conditions. The court found no violation of constitutional rights and emphasized the importance of quality in public procurement.

Case overview
- The case is Abhijit Saikia vs The State of Assam and 3 others, heard in the Gauhati High Court on March 19, 2024. 
- The petitioner, Abhijit Saikia, filed an application under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.PC) seeking to quash an FIR registered against him. 

Key facts
- The FIR (Gossaigaon P.S. Case No. 383/2023) was registered under Sections 420, 406, 468 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and Section 13(1) of the Assam Cattle Preservation Act, 2021. 
- The FIR alleges that on November 29, 2023, a vehicle carrying beef disguised as buffalo meat was intercepted. 
- The vehicle was found to contain meat that was later confirmed to be beef by the Directorate of Forensic Science and Laboratory. 
- Abhijit Saikia is the owner of Eden Cold Storage, where the meat was allegedly stored and sold. 

Legal issues and arguments
- The petitioner argues that he has been operating his cold storage business legally and has a valid FSSAI license. 
- He contends that the investigation was improperly conducted, claiming that only a food analyst is authorized to examine food under the FSSAI Act. 
- The petitioner asserts that the police officer acted beyond his jurisdiction and that the meat in question was frozen buffalo meat, not freshly slaughtered beef. 
- He claims that the seizure of his cold storage and the meat has caused him significant financial loss and that he was subjected to inhumane treatment by the police. 

Court's reasoning
- The court noted that the petitioner is charged under multiple sections of the IPC and the Cattle Preservation Act, but there is no specific allegation of criminal breach of trust (Section 406 IPC). 
- The court referenced a Supreme Court decision stating that police cannot seize immovable property, which applies to the cold storage in this case. 
- The court found that the police officer lacked jurisdiction to seal the cold storage, which is classified as immovable property. 

Decision or judgment
- The court ordered the immediate removal of the lock and seal from the Eden Cold Storage. 
- The court refrained from making any orders regarding the seized beef or the investigation process at this time. 
- No stay on the investigation was granted, and the matter is to be listed again in two weeks.

column3: The case involves M/s Jubilant Foodworks Ltd., a company operating a Domino's Pizza outlet in Delhi, and Sh. Bal Mukund, a Food Safety Officer. The food safety department sampled 'Corn Flour' from the outlet's kitchen area, which was used as a dusting agent during pizza preparation. The Food Analyst later found the sample to be sub-standard due to high ash content and alcoholic acidity. The appellants argued that the sampled product was 'corn meal' and not 'corn flour,' and that it was not intended for sale directly to customers but for internal kitchen use. They also claimed they were not responsible for the manufacturing or storage of the sample product and that the sample was not representative, among other defenses. The respondent imposed a penalty of Rs. 2 lakhs on the appellants for violations related to sub-standard food use and storage, leading to this appeal.

column15: Case overview: The case involves an appeal filed by M/s Jubilant Foodworks Ltd and Sh. Akash Tyagi against Sh. Bal Mukund, a Food Safety Officer, challenging an order dated 20.08.2018 that imposed a penalty of Rs. 2 Lakhs for violations of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and related regulations. The appeal was heard in the Food Safety Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi, on 02.03.2023, with the judgment delivered on 13.03.2023. Key facts: 1. The appellants operate a Domino's Pizza restaurant where a sample of 'Corn Meal' was taken by the FSO on 07.05.2014, which was later reported as 'sub-standard' by the Food Analyst due to excessive ash content. 2. The appellants argued that 'Corn Meal' is not the same as 'Corn Flour' and is used as a dusting agent, not for direct sale. 3. The appellants claimed the FSO misidentified the product and did not take samples from sealed packets. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The appellants contended that the Adjudicating Officer accepted the FSO's complaint without proper verification and misapplied the standards for 'Corn Flour' to 'Corn Meal'. 2. They argued that the sample was not meant for direct sale and that they were not responsible for the product's quality as they were end-users. 3. The appellants sought to implead the supplier of the product, but this request was denied by the Adjudicating Officer. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found no merit in the appellants' claims, stating that the sample was indeed 'Corn Flour' and not 'Corn Meal', and that it was used in the cooking process, thus falling under the definition of food as per the FSS Act. 2. The court upheld the findings of the Food Analyst and the Referral Laboratory, which confirmed the sample was sub-standard. 3. The court noted that the appellants failed to provide evidence regarding the supplier and that the FSO acted within his powers to take the sample. 4. The court dismissed the relevance of the appellants' cited case law, stating they were based on the previous Food Adulteration Act and not applicable under the FSS Act. Decision or judgment: The appeal was dismissed, and the penalty of Rs. 2 Lakhs was upheld. The court ordered the release of the FDR submitted by the appellants to the department for penalty realization and directed the return of the original record to the Adjudicating Officer.

column15: Case overview: The case involves Lakhmi Chand challenging his conviction under the Food Safety and Standard Act of 2006. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh heard the case on August 24, 2023, where Lakhmi Chand sought suspension of his jail sentence and bail. The petitioner was convicted and sentenced to two months of rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 10,000. Key facts: 1. Lakhmi Chand was convicted under Section 3(zz), 26(2)(i) read with Section 59(1) of the Food Safety and Standard Act of 2006. 2. The conviction was based on the collection of food samples by Food Inspectors, which were allegedly collected in polythene bags instead of the prescribed containers. 3. The petitioner argued that the lower courts did not properly appreciate the evidence and committed an error in convicting him. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner contended that the collection method of food samples violated the rules set forth in the Food Safety and Standard Act. 2. The petitioner requested suspension of the sentence, citing the short duration of the sentence and the potential delay in the final disposal of the revision. 3. The State's counsel opposed the application for suspension of the sentence, seeking its dismissal. Court's reasoning: 1. The court considered the facts and circumstances of the case, including the short sentence and the arguments presented by the petitioner. 2. Without commenting on the merits of the case, the court found sufficient grounds to allow the application for suspension of the sentence. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the application for suspension of the sentence, directing that Lakhmi Chand be released on bail upon depositing the fine amount and furnishing a personal bond of Rs. 50,000 with a solvent surety. The petitioner is required to appear before the Registry of the Court on October 18, 2023, and on other dates as may be fixed until the final disposal of the revision.

The petitioner claims the alleged offence occurred on 30.10.2015, but the Magistrate took cognizance only on 19.01.2017, which is beyond the limitation period. 3. The respondent contends that the complaint was filed within one year of the alleged offence and that all procedures were followed. Court's reasoning: 1. The court examined whether the mandatory provisions of Section 42(3) of the FSSA 2006 were followed. 2. It was found that the Designated Officer sent recommendations for prosecution nearly eight months after receiving the report, violating the 14-day requirement. 3. The court referenced previous cases where similar violations led to quashing of complaints. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the Criminal Original Petition and quashed the proceedings against the petitioner, concluding that the complaint could not be sustained due to the violation of mandatory provisions.

column15:
Case overview
- The case is titled Dharampal Satyapal Limited vs The State Of Jharkhand Through The Chief, heard in the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi under W.P.(C) No.3026 of 2021. 
- The petitioners are Dharampal Satyapal Limited and Saroj Tradecom Private Limited, represented by their directors. 
- The respondents include the State of Jharkhand, the Principal Secretary-cum-Commissioner of Food Safety, and the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.

Key facts
- The petitioners sought to quash notifications dated 08.05.2020 and 28.05.2021, which imposed a prohibition on the manufacture, storage, distribution, or sale of "Rajnigandha" Pan Masala for one year each, citing the presence of Magnesium Carbonate in samples from 2019-2020.
- The petitioners argued that the prohibitions constituted double jeopardy as they were subjected to punitive action twice for the same issue.
- The notifications were previously challenged in a separate writ petition (W.P.(C) No.3346 of 2022), which was decided on 28.08.2023.

Legal issues and arguments
- The primary legal issue was whether the notifications issued under section 30(2)(a) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, were valid, given that they had already been quashed by a prior court order.
- The petitioners requested the court to issue a writ of certiorari to quash the notifications and to produce the case records.

Court's reasoning
- The court noted that the notifications dated 08.05.2020 and 28.05.2021 had already been quashed by the Division Bench in the earlier writ petition, thus rendering the current petition moot.
- The court emphasized that since the notifications were quashed at the instance of the petitioners, there was no need for further orders in the present writ petition.

Decision or judgment
- The writ petition was disposed of in accordance with the order dated 28.08.2023 from W.P.(C) No.3346 of 2022, confirming the quashing of the prohibitory notifications. 
- Any pending interlocutory applications were also disposed of.

column15: Case overview: The case involves an appeal by Kailash Chand Pandey and others against the Food Safety Officer, Naresh Kumar Sharma, regarding a penalty imposed for violations of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The appeal was heard on November 28, 2023, and the judgment was delivered on the same day. The appellants challenged an order from December 30, 2022, which held them responsible for misbranding and imposed penalties. Key facts: 1. On October 15, 2018, a sample of 'Foxnuts' was taken from the appellants, which was later found to be misbranded by the Food Analyst's report dated October 29, 2018. 2. The misbranding was attributed to the failure to declare the 'best before' date in capital letters, violating several provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. 3. The Adjudicating Officer imposed penalties of Rs. 25,000 on appellants 1 to 5 and 7, and Rs. 50,000 on appellants 6 and 8. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The appellants argued that the labeling defect was minor and should not have resulted in adjudication proceedings, as per the FSSAI's advisory letters dated July 17, 2018, and January 17, 2020, which suggested that minor labeling defects should be addressed through improvement notices rather than penalties. 2. The appellants contended that the Food Safety Officer failed to follow proper procedures and that the report of the Food Analyst lacked evidentiary value. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the labeling defect regarding the 'best before' date was categorized as insignificant and should have been addressed through an improvement notice under Section 32 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. 2. The court emphasized that the Food Safety Officer did not issue an improvement notice as required, and the subsequent regulations in 2020 had removed the requirement for the 'best before' date to be in capital letters. 3. The court found that the Adjudicating Officer failed to consider the FSSAI's advisories and the nature of the labeling defect. Decision or judgment: The court set aside the impugned order of the Adjudicating Officer, stating that the penalties were improperly imposed. The complaint pertains to the alleged unsafe packaged drinking water. The applications were heard together due to common questions of fact and law. Key facts: 1. The complaint was filed based on a sample of packaged drinking water collected on July 30, 2013, which was later found to be sub-standard and unsafe. 2. The petitioners claimed they were not directors of the accused company at the time of the alleged offence, as they had resigned prior to the sample collection date. 3. The petitioners argued that they cannot be held vicariously liable under Section 66 of the FSSAI Act as they were not in charge of the company at the time of the offence. 2. They contended that the learned Magistrate failed to follow the mandatory procedure under Section 202(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which requires an inquiry before issuing process against accused residing outside the jurisdiction. 3. The respondents argued that the FSSAI Act is a special statute and the complaint was valid as the packaged water was found unsafe. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the petitioners were not directors of the company at the time of the alleged offence, and thus could not be held responsible under the FSSAI Act. 2. The court noted that the complaint did not attribute any specific role to the petitioners regarding the alleged unsafe product. 3. The court emphasized that the provisions of the FSSAI Act do not negate the need for proper attribution of responsibility to individuals in a company. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the petitions and quashed the impugned complaint and the summoning order against the petitioners, concluding that they were not responsible for the alleged offence.

On October 31, 2013, a Food Safety Officer inspected the establishment and found unsafe food articles, specifically Khoya Roll, which lacked proper labeling. 3. A sample was taken and analyzed, revealing excessive synthetic dye and the presence of aluminum leaves, deemed injurious to health. 4. The prosecution was initiated based on the analysis report, leading to Singh's conviction on March 12, 2020, for violating Section 26(2)(i) of the Food Safety and Standards Act. 5. Singh was sentenced to three months of simple imprisonment and fined Rs. 50,000, with an additional month of imprisonment for defaulting on the fine. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The prosecution was tasked with proving that the testing method employed was valid under the regulations. Court's reasoning: 1. The court acknowledged that while findings from the RFL are generally not questioned, the method of analysis could be scrutinized for compliance with mandatory provisions. 2. The court noted that additional evidence was necessary to determine if the testing method used by the RFL was appropriate. 3. The burden of proof regarding the validity of the testing method lay with the prosecution. Decision or judgment: The court set aside the conviction and sentence, remanding the case back to the Trial Court for additional evidence to be recorded. column15: Case overview: The case involves an appeal filed by M/s. Devyani International Ltd. and its representatives against the State of Delhi regarding a conviction under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The appellants challenge an order dated June 2, 2021, which imposed penalties for violations related to food labeling and misbranding. The appeal was filed on July 15, 2021, and the judgment was delivered on February 24, 2023. Key facts: 1. The appellants include M/s. Devyani International Ltd., its nominees, and a restaurant manager from a Pizza Hut outlet. 2. The complaint arose from an inspection on June 21, 2018, where a Food Safety Officer purchased a sample of 'Fusilli Barilli (Pasta)' and later reported it as misbranded. 3. The Adjudicating Officer found the appellants guilty of multiple violations under the FSS Act and imposed fines totaling Rs. 80,000. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The appellants argue that the complaint was barred by limitation as the Adjudicating Officer took cognizance after one year from the alleged offense. 2. They contend that they were not responsible for the labeling of the product as they purchased it from an importer and were bona fide consumers. 3. The appellants claim protection under Section 80(B)(2)(d)(i) of the FSS Act, asserting they cannot be held liable for misbranding. 4. The Adjudicating Officer's order is criticized for being mechanical and lacking legal basis. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found that the Adjudicating Officer's order could not be sustained as the appellants were not the producers or manufacturers of the food item. 2. The court noted that the food item was not meant for direct sale to consumers, thus not falling under the relevant sections of the FSS Act. 3. The court emphasized that the appellants had no role in the labeling and that the prosecution was unwarranted and an abuse of process. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the appeal, set aside the impugned order dated June 2, 2021, and directed that the original record be sent back to the Adjudicating Officer. The appeal was deemed valid, and the penalties imposed were overturned.

column3: The case involves the petitioners IMC Limited and Indian Oil Corporation Limited contesting the authority of the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) to regulate pipelines laid by entities for their own use without obtaining authorization. IMC Limited had received authorization from PNGRB in 2015 to lay a pipeline from Ennore Port to Manali Industrial Area. In 2023, Indian Oil started laying pipelines for transportation from its jetty to its terminal and to Vellur Terminal for resale purposes without PNGRB's authorization, leading PNGRB to direct IOCL to stop its construction. IMC Limited sought court intervention to direct IOCL to halt the unauthorized pipelines and to seek penalties for violations. IOCL argued that its pipelines for transporting its own petroleum do not require PNGRB approval, claiming such pipelines are outside the regulator's jurisdiction. The petitioner contended that post the enactment of the PNGRB Act, all pipelines for transportation, including self-use pipelines, should be regulated as common or contract carriers, and that captive pipelines are no longer recognized under the law. The court examined whether pipelines laid solely for a company's own transportation require PNGRB approval, ultimately ruling that the Act does not prohibit entities from laying pipelines for their own use and that such captive pipelines do not fall within the regulator's jurisdiction. The court set aside PNGRB's directive to IOCL and dismissed IMC's petition.

The case involves two writ petitions concerning the regulation of pipelines for transportation of petroleum and petroleum products under the PNGRB Act, 2006. The petitioner, IMC Limited, and Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL) challenge the authority of the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) to regulate pipelines laid for self-use or captive purposes by entities like IOCL. The core legal issue is whether, after the enactment of the PNGRB Act, entities can lay captive pipelines without authorization from the PNGRB.

The court examines the legislative intent, statutory definitions, and regulations under the PNGRB Act. It notes that the Act primarily regulates pipelines declared as common carrier or contract carrier, which are meant for transportation by more than one entity on a non-discriminatory basis. The Act does not explicitly prohibit or regulate pipelines laid solely for an entity's own use (captive pipelines). The court emphasizes that the Act and its regulations focus on promoting competition, fair access, and preventing infructuous investments, primarily through the regulation of common and contract carrier pipelines.

The petitioners argue that the concept of captive pipelines has been abolished or rendered obsolete by the PNGRB Act, citing provisions and regulations that define and regulate pipelines for multiple users. The respondents, including the Union of India and PNGRB, contend that the Act does not explicitly prohibit captive pipelines and that such pipelines are outside the scope of PNGRB regulation.

The court reviews relevant statutory provisions, regulations, and judicial precedents, concluding that the PNGRB Act does not expressly prohibit entities from laying pipelines for their own use. It states that the absence of a specific prohibition means that such pipelines are not within the regulatory ambit of the PNGRB. The court also notes that the regulations, including the 2010 and 2012 Regulations, focus on pipelines that are declared as common or contract carriers, not on dedicated or captive pipelines.

The court observes that the legislative scheme aims to regulate pipelines that impact multiple entities and consumers, and that the concept of captive pipelines remains valid unless explicitly legislated out of existence. It emphasizes that the power to declare existing pipelines as common or contract carriers under Section 20 of the PNGRB Act is limited to pipelines that are not solely for self-use.

In conclusion, the court sets aside the communication issued by the PNGRB directing IOCL to stop laying pipelines without authorization, ruling that IOCL is permitted to lay pipelines for its own use without prior approval from the PNGRB. The petition filed by IMC Limited is dismissed, and the challenge to the PNGRB's authority is rejected, affirming that captive pipelines are outside the regulatory scope of the PNGRB Act.

The petitioners made detailed allegations about non-disclosure of biosafety data, inadequate risk evaluation, potential contamination of natural gene pools, and violations of the precautionary principle, pointing out that the approval was ultimately based on foreign studies, insufficient local research, and procedural lapses. The government and GEAC defend the approval as lawful, scientifically justified, and compliant with environmental safeguards, emphasizing the importance of technology for agricultural productivity and food security and asserting that the procedures were followed properly. The core issue is whether the approval process was lawful, transparent, based on sound science, and consistent with constitutional and international environmental principles.

The case involves petitions challenging the environmental approval granted by the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC) and the Union of India for the release of genetically modified (GM) mustard hybrid DMH-11. The petitioners, including Gene Campaign, argue that the approval process was flawed, lacked transparency, and violated constitutional principles, including the right to a safe environment under Article 21, and the precautionary principle. The petitions also challenge the constitutionality of the 1989 Rules governing GMOs, citing issues of delegation, arbitrariness, and procedural lapses.

The Supreme Court examined the legal framework, including the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the 1989 Rules, and international protocols like the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety. It reviewed the procedural history, including multiple orders and the appointment of Technical Expert Committees (TECs) to assess biosafety and environmental risks.

The Court found that the approval process was flawed, noting that the GEAC delegated its core function to sub-committees and expert groups without proper application of mind, and that the decision was taken without adequate scientific and environmental risk assessment, especially regarding long-term and transgenerational effects. The Court observed that the process violated the precautionary principle, which mandates caution in the face of scientific uncertainty, especially for GMOs intended for environmental release.

The Court also highlighted deficiencies in the regulatory framework, including lack of independent verification, transparency, stakeholder participation, and proper assessment of socio-economic and environmental impacts. It emphasized that the approval was not based on sufficient indigenous data, especially given India‚Äôs status as a center of origin and diversity for mustard.

The Court held that the conditional approval granted by GEAC and the subsequent decision by the Union of India were vitiated, and thus, set aside the approval. It directed that future approvals should be based on a clear, transparent process involving independent scientific assessment, public participation, and adherence to international biosafety protocols. The Court also emphasized the need for a comprehensive national policy on GMOs, proper labelling of GM foods, and the establishment of robust regulatory and biosafety infrastructure.

The judgment underscores that while scientific and technological progress is vital, it must be balanced with environmental safety, public health, and constitutional rights, following the principles of sustainable development, precaution, and intergenerational equity.

Case overview:
The case involves Dharampalsatyapal Limited, a manufacturer of pan masala, challenging the prosecution initiated against it under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The case was heard in the High Court of Kerala, with the petitioner represented by Mr. Shivakumar V.R. and the respondents being the State of Kerala and the Commissioner of Food Safety.

Key facts:
- The petitioner is accused in four criminal cases pending before the Chief Judicial Magistrate's Court in Palakkad, related to violations of the Food Safety and Standards Act.
- The products in question were found to contain Magnesium Carbonate, and in one case, Monosodium Glutamate, which led to the prosecution.
- The initial seizure of the pan masala occurred on April 28, 2013, and the analysis report was received on September 20, 2013, indicating the presence of Magnesium Carbonate but not nicotine or tobacco.
- The Commissioner of Food Safety sanctioned prosecution on August 11, 2015, citing procedural and administrative delays as reasons for extending the time limit for prosecution.

Legal issues and arguments:
- The primary legal issue was whether the time limit for taking cognizance of offences under Section 77 of the Food Safety and Standards Act could be extended based on procedural and administrative delays.
- The petitioner argued that the reasons provided for the delay were vague and insufficient, failing to meet the statutory requirement for written reasons.
- The respondents contended that the time limit should be interpreted flexibly to avoid stifling prosecutions under the Act, referencing Section 41(2) of the Act and provisions of the Cr.P.C.

Court's reasoning:
- The court emphasized that Section 77 of the Act mandates a strict one-year limit for prosecution, extendable to three years only with valid written reasons.
- The court found the reasons provided by the Commissioner to be inadequate, as they did not specify the nature of the procedural and administrative delays.
- Citing precedents, the court noted that vague terms like "procedural and administrative delay" do not constitute valid reasons for extending the prosecution period.
- The court highlighted the importance of timely action by food inspectors to ensure fair legal processes and protect individual liberties.

Decision or judgment:
- The court quashed the proceedings against Dharampalsatyapal Limited in all four cases (S.T. No. 622/2015, S.T. No. 623/2015, S.T. No. 624/2015, and S.T. No. 52/2016) due to the invalidity of the prosecution sanction based on insufficient reasons for delay.
- The court ruled that the complaints filed in these cases were legally invalid and allowed the criminal miscellaneous cases filed by the petitioner.

The petitioners challenge the exclusion of Bachelor in Pharmacy (B. Pharmacy) and Master in Pharmacy (M. Pharmacy) as qualifications for the new post, arguing it is arbitrary and illegal. Key facts: 1. The petitioners are currently working as pharmacists in various health centers in Rajasthan. 2. The previous post of Food Inspector required B. Pharmacy and M. Pharmacy as qualifications, but the new post of Food Safety Officer does not include these qualifications. 3. The petitioners argue that the duties of Food Safety Officers are similar to those of Food Inspectors. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioners contend that the change in qualifications is arbitrary since the nature of duties remains largely the same. 2. They argue that their qualifications should be considered equivalent to those prescribed under the new rules. 3. The respondents maintain that the rule-making authority has the discretion to set eligibility criteria and that the qualifications for Food Safety Officer are distinct from those of Food Inspector. Court's reasoning: 1. The court found no merit in the challenge to the constitutionality and validity of the rules, stating that it is within the jurisdiction of the rule-making authority to prescribe qualifications. 2. The court noted that the duties and responsibilities of Food Safety Officers may differ from those of Food Inspectors, justifying the change in qualifications. 3. The court emphasized that equivalence of qualifications is a matter for experts and the competent authority to determine. Decision or judgment: The court dismissed the writ petition without notice to the other party, upholding the validity of the impugned notifications and the qualifications prescribed for the post of Food Safety Officer.

Case overview
- The case is titled D.Nadarajan vs The Food Safety Officer, Crl.O.P.(MD)No.18126 of 2022, heard by the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court on 24 April 2024.
- The petitioner, D.Nadarajan, is the accused No.1, and the respondent is the Food Safety Officer.

Key facts
- On 25 August 2020, the Food Safety Officers took food samples of Groundnut Oil from Natarajan's Grocery Shop, owned by the petitioner.
- The samples were sent to the Food Analyst, who reported on 19 October 2020 that the samples were substandard.
- The Designated Officer sent a notice to the petitioner on 28 October 2020 regarding the substandard report.
- The petitioner filed an appeal under Section 46(4) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, but the Designated Officer did not forward the sample to a referral laboratory or decide the appeal within the stipulated time.

Legal issues and arguments
- The petitioner argued that the failure of the Designated Officer to dispose of the appeal and forward the sample to the referral lab violated the Food Safety and Standards Act, specifically Rule 2.4.6.
- The respondent contended that the petitioner should have filed the appeal in Form-VIII instead of Form-VII, which was the basis for objecting to the quashing of the proceedings.

Court's reasoning
- The court reviewed the records and noted that the petitioner filed the appeal on 23 November 2020, which was acknowledged by the Designated Officer on 24 November 2020, after the notice was received on 28 October 2020.
- The court found that the appeal was filed beyond the 30-day limit as required by the Food Safety and Standards Act, but the Designated Officer's failure to decide the appeal within the time frame constituted a violation of the Act.
- The court concluded that the prosecution was unsustainable due to the Designated Officer's inaction.

Decision or judgment
- The court quashed the Criminal Proceedings in S.T.C.No.667 of 2021 against the petitioner, D.Nadarajan, and allowed the Criminal Original Petition.
- The connected Miscellaneous Petitions were also closed.

column15: Case overview: The case involves an appeal filed by Rajesh Juneja against the judgment and order on sentence dated 18.01.2017, where he was convicted under Section 16 (1) (a) of the PFA Act for misbranding a food product. The appeal was decided on 04.08.2022 by Additional Sessions Judge Harjyot Singh Bhalla at Patiala House Courts, New Delhi. Key facts: 1. Rajesh Juneja operated M/s Shri Balaji Food Products. 2. On 18.06.2008, a food inspector seized 200 grams of Roasted Namkeen from the establishment, which was later found to be misbranded according to PFA Rules, despite conforming to quality standards. 3. A complaint was filed on 09.09.2008, leading to the trial and subsequent conviction of Juneja. 4. The trial court imposed a fine of Rs. 25,000 and a one-month imprisonment in default of payment. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The main issue was whether the product's labeling violated PFA Rules, specifically regarding the declaration of the 'best before' date. 2. Juneja's counsel cited a precedent case where the use of the word 'within' in labeling was deemed acceptable. 3. The defense argued that Juneja had purchased the product from a licensed dealer and provided a bill, which should exempt him from liability under Section 19 (2) of the PFA Act. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the trial court failed to consider the defense under Section 19 (2) of the PFA Act, which protects vendors who purchase food products from licensed dealers. 2. The court emphasized that the existence of a bill or cash memo suffices as a warranty, even if it lacks specific details. 3. The court found that the food inspector did not adequately verify the bill provided by Juneja, which was crucial for establishing his defense. 4. The court referenced previous judgments that supported the notion that small retailers are often unfairly penalized while larger entities evade scrutiny. Decision or judgment: The court acquitted Rajesh Juneja, concluding that he was entitled to the defense under Section 19 (2) of the PFA Act, and did not address the issue of prior departmental warnings for misbranding.

Case overview: The case involves an appeal by Sh. Shatrughan Singh, proprietor of M/s Tomar Paneer Bhandar, against an order dated 22.04.2022 by the Adjudicating Officer, imposing a penalty of Rs. One Lakh for violating the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSS Act). The appeal was filed under Section 70 of the FSS Act. The respondent is Sh. Bal Mukund, a Food Safety Officer. The judgment was delivered on 04.08.2023. 

Key facts: 1. On 07.10.2017, a sample of 'Paneer' was collected from the appellant's premises for analysis. 2. The sample was found to exceed the maximum moisture limit of 60% as per the Food Analyst's report dated 12.10.2017. 3. The appellant did not file an appeal against the Food Analyst's report within the stipulated period. 4. The Adjudicating Officer found the appellant guilty of selling a substandard food article and imposed a penalty. 

Legal issues and arguments: 1. The appellant contended that the Adjudicating Officer misinterpreted the relevant sections of the FSS Act and failed to consider that the sample was taken before the new moisture specification of 60% was operationalized. 2. The appellant argued that the moisture specification was 70% at the time of sampling, as the amendment was notified on 13.10.2017 and came into effect on 01.07.2018. 3. The respondent did not file a reply to the appeal. 

Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the FSSAI's revised standards were in operation when the sample was taken, but the notification regarding compliance came into effect on 01.07.2018. 2. The court found that the Adjudicating Officer did not consider the timing of the moisture specification when imposing the penalty. 3. The court concluded that the penalty was unjustified as the moisture limit of 70% was applicable at the time of sampling. 

Decision or judgment: The court accepted the appeal and set aside the impugned order dated 22.04.2022, thereby nullifying the penalty imposed on the appellant. The record of the Adjudicating Officer was ordered to be sent back, and the appeal file was to be consigned to the Record Room.

Case overview
- The case involves Deepak Agarwal and another petitioner against the State of Telangana, concerning Criminal Petition Nos. 6681 and 7309 of 2019.
- The petitions are filed to quash proceedings in Crime No. 164 of 2019 registered at Dabeerpura Police Station, Hyderabad.

Key facts
- The complaint was lodged by the Superintendent of Jails, Central Prison, Chanchalguda, Hyderabad, on 19.10.2019, alleging that the petitioners, as contractors for supplying food and ration items to the jail, supplied adulterated sunflower oil.

Legal issues and arguments
- The petitioners argue that the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (FSSA Act) provides a specific legal framework for dealing with food adulteration, and therefore, no prosecution under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) can be initiated.
- The petitioners cite the Supreme Court judgment in Ram Nath v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which states that simultaneous prosecution under IPC and FSSA is not permissible.
- Additional judgments from the Allahabad High Court and Patna High Court are referenced, supporting the argument that the FSSA Act has an overriding effect on other laws regarding food adulteration.

Court's reasoning
- The court agrees with the petitioners' argument that the FSSA Act has an overriding effect on general laws concerning food adulteration, thus barring prosecution under IPC provisions.
- The court notes that the learned Additional Public Prosecutor suggested the possibility of prosecuting under the FSSA Act, but highlights that under Section 77 of the FSSA Act, no court can take cognizance of an offence after one year from the date of the offence, extendable to three years only under specific conditions.
- Since the complaint was made almost four years after the alleged offence, the court finds that prosecution under the FSSA Act is also barred due to the time limitation.

Decision or judgment
- The court allows both criminal petitions and quashes the proceedings against the petitioners in Crime No. 164 of 2019 at Dabeerpura Police Station, Hyderabad. 
- Any pending miscellaneous applications are closed.

Case overview
- The case is titled B.Selvakumar vs State by Food Safety Officer, adjudicated in the High Court of Judicature at Madras on 5 March 2024. 
- The petitioner, B.Selvakumar, filed a Criminal Original Petition (Crl.O.P.No.3406 of 2022) under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash proceedings in C.C.No.2796 of 2021 pending before the IX Metropolitan Magistrate, Saidapet.

Key facts
- The prosecution alleges violations of Sections 52(1) and 59(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. 
- The complainant, a food safety officer, inspected M/s. Cheers Ventures on 27 February 2019 and purchased 6 packets of Raja Snacks Mixture for analysis. 
- The analysis revealed the product contained Tartrazine, an unauthorized coloring agent, and was misbranded, violating specific food safety regulations. 
- The complaint was filed after obtaining necessary sanctions from the Commissioner of the Food Safety Department.

Legal issues and arguments
- The petitioner contends he is merely a seller and not liable for the alleged offenses, as the manufacturer (A3) should be held accountable under Section 27(3) of the Act. 
- The petitioner argues that the product was licensed for sale by FSSAI and that he had no knowledge of its unsafe nature. 
- The petitioner cites previous case law to support his claim that liability should not extend to sellers without knowledge of unsafe products.

Court's reasoning
- The court noted that the seller is liable under Section 27(3) if the product is misbranded or unsafe, regardless of whether they had knowledge of the product's condition. 
- The court found that the food analysis report indicated the product was misbranded and unsafe, which prima facie establishes liability for the seller. 
- The court acknowledged the delay in analysis but stated that it could be addressed during the trial, and valid communication regarding the delay must be proven in court.

Decision or judgment
- The High Court dismissed the petitioner's request to quash the proceedings in C.C.No.2796 of 2021, allowing the case to proceed in the trial court. 
- The petitioner was granted liberty to seek remedies before the trial court. 
- The connected miscellaneous petitions were also closed.

Amit C Jain, proprietor of Vijay Modis Tea House, against the Food Safety Inspector and the Designated Officer of the Department of Food Safety and Standards, Kalaburagi. The petitioner seeks to quash an order dated December 29, 2015, which imposed a fine for misbranding of instant noodles under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The petition was heard and reserved on August 29, 2023, and the judgment was pronounced on October 12, 2023. Key facts: 1. The petitioner manufactures and markets instant noodles under the brand name 'Sunfeast Yippee! Noodles'. 2. On June 8, 2015, a sample of the noodles was collected by the Food Safety Inspector, which was later reported as misbranded due to the label stating 'No Added MSG'. 3. The petitioner contended that they were not provided with proper notice or the right to appeal against the Food Analyst's report. 4. The Designated Officer imposed a fine of Rs. 10,000 based on the Food Analyst's report. Legal issues and arguments: 1. The petitioner argued that the product complied with all requirements and that the misbranding claim was unfounded, as there was no evidence of MSG being added. 2. The petitioner claimed that the prosecution was initiated without proper inspection of the manufacturing premises to ascertain if MSG was added. 3. The respondents contended that the label's claim of 'No Added MSG' justified the prosecution. Court's reasoning: 1. The court noted that the Food Analyst's report indicated compliance with standards but also stated the product was misbranded due to the label. 2. The court highlighted that there is no analytical method to determine if MSG was added during manufacturing, and prosecution should not occur without such determination. 3. The court found that the Designated Officer did not inspect the manufacturing unit, which was necessary to ascertain the claim of misbranding. 4. The court emphasized that the petitioner was not given the right to appeal as mandated by Section 46(4) of the Act, violating principles of natural justice. Decision or judgment: The court allowed the writ petition and quashed the impugned order passed by the Additional District Magistrate cum Adjudicating Authority in C.C.No.316/203/55/2015-16, thereby dismissing the prosecution against the petitioner.

The case involved arguments over the correctness of the confiscation, interpretation of origin documents, and the legality of the Tribunal's decision to permit re-export instead of confiscation.

Case overview
- The case involves two Customs Appeals (CUSAP No. 4 and 5 of 2024) filed by the Commissioner of Customs, Ludhiana against M/s Star Spices and M/s Sherry Network Private Limited. 
- The appeals challenge the order of the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) dated 07.06.2024, which set aside the absolute confiscation of Areca Nuts imported by the respondents and allowed their re-export on payment of a fine.

Key facts
- The respondents imported Areca Nuts claiming exemption from customs duty under the Indo-Sri Lanka Free Trade Agreement notification dated 01.03.2023.
- The Revenue suspected that the respondents mixed Areca Nuts of Sri Lankan origin with those from outside the SAARC territory to evade customs duty.
- Samples of the imported Areca Nuts were tested and found to be substandard and unsafe for human consumption according to the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
- The adjudicating authority ordered absolute confiscation of the goods, which was upheld by the appellate authority before being set aside by CESTAT.

Legal issues and arguments
- The main legal issue was whether the CESTAT erred in setting aside the order of absolute confiscation and allowing re-export.
- The appellant argued that the confiscation was justified due to fraudulent mis-declaration of the country of origin and that the goods were unfit for consumption.
- The respondents contended that they complied with all import regulations and that the goods were certified as fit for human consumption by the Port Health Officer.

Court's reasoning
- The CESTAT found that the goods were unfit for human consumption but could be used for industrial purposes, thus justifying re-export.
- The court noted that the evidence of mis-declaration was based on outdated communications and did not pertain to the current import.
- The court emphasized that allowing re-export would prevent financial loss and waste of foreign exchange.
- The CESTAT's decision to reduce the penalty and allow re-export was deemed reasonable and within its jurisdiction.

Decision or judgment
- The High Court dismissed the appeals filed by the Revenue, affirming the CESTAT's order allowing re-export of the Areca Nuts on payment of a fine of Rs. 25 lakhs and reducing the penalty to Rs. 10 lakhs.
- The court ordered that the goods be allowed to be re-exported forthwith.

Case overview
- Case Title: A. Biswanath Patra vs State Of Odisha & Ors.
- Court: High Court of Orissa at Cuttack
- Date of Judgment: 5 February 2024
- Bench: Acting Chief Justice Dr. B.R. Sarangi and Mr. Justice Murahari Sri Raman

Key facts
- The petitioner, A. Biswanath Patra, filed a writ petition seeking to quash order no.138 dated 02.01.2024 (Annexure-5), which extended the time for receipt of applications for registration as approved suppliers for food grains and other articles.
- The original tender call notice (Annexure-1) required bidders to have a valid Food License under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

Legal issues and arguments
- The petitioner argued that the corrigendum issued on 02.01.2024, which modified the requirement to include a valid Registration Certificate or Food License, was not legally sustainable.
- The State, represented by Mr. P.K. Muduli, contended that the modification was necessary to clarify the requirements and to allow more bidders to participate.

Court's reasoning
- The court noted that the original clause in the tender call notice was indeed clarified by the corrigendum, which did not change the essence of the requirement but rather aimed to eliminate confusion.
- The court found that the extension of the application deadline to 06.02.2024 would not prejudice any party involved.

Decision or judgment
- The court dismissed the writ petition, finding no illegality or irregularity in the issuance of the corrigendum under Annexure-5.
